en.title: Identifying people and things
en.tip: Use questo (this) or quello (that) to point to something, or è + a noun to name it. To give someone's name, say si chiama followed by the name. These short patterns are all you need at this level.
en.why_this_matters: You will need to identify things constantly — in a shop, a classroom, or when meeting new people. Knowing how to point and name lets you communicate even when your vocabulary is limited.
en.explanation: ## Identifying people and things This function is about pointing out or naming a person or object so your listener knows exactly what or who you mean. ### Key patterns **Pointing words (demonstratives)** | Italian | English | |---|---| | questo / questa | this (near you) | | questi / queste | these (near you) | | quello / quella | that (far from you) | | quelli / quelle | those (far from you) | Example: Vorrei questo. — 'I would like this one.' (pointing at something in a shop) **Naming with è** Use è + noun group to say what something or someone is: - È la mia professoressa. — 'She is my teacher.' - Questo è un dizionario. — 'This is a dictionary.' **Giving a name with si chiama** Use si chiama + name to say what someone is called: - Lui si chiama Mario. — 'His name is Mario.' - Lei si chiama Sofia. — 'Her name is Sofia.' For a plural subject, use si chiamano: Si chiamano Luca e Anna. ### Register These patterns work in both formal and informal situations. The words questo and quello are neutral — you can use them with a teacher or a friend. ### Cultural note In Italian shops and markets, pointing and saying questo, per favore is a perfectly normal and polite way to order or buy something, especially when you do not yet know the word for the item. ### Common mistakes - **Gender agreement**: questo and quello must match the noun — questo libro (masculine) but questa borsa (feminine). Check the noun's gender first. - **Confusing questo and quello**: Use questo for things close to you and quello for things further away — just like 'this' and 'that' in English. - **Dropping si**: Do not say chiama Mario — the full form si chiama Mario is required.

en.title: Making a simple statement
en.tip: Use a verb like essere or abitare with a noun, adjective, or place to state a fact. You can also say a full sentence like Non ho capito to report what happened. Keep it short and direct.
en.why_this_matters: Asserting facts is one of the most basic things you do in any language — telling people who you are, where you live, or what is happening. Without this function, you cannot share information or take part in even the simplest conversation.
en.explanation: ## Making a Simple Statement (Asserting) Asserting means stating a fact or piece of information. It is the building block of almost every conversation. ### When to use this function Use it any time you want to share information — about yourself, another person, an object, or a situation. ### Key patterns **Noun / adjective statements with essere (to be):** | Italian | English | |---|---| | Sono uno studente. | I am a student. | | Sono stanco. | I am tired. | | È una bella città. | It is a beautiful city. | **Full-sentence statements:** | Italian | English | |---|---| | Abito a Milano. | I live in Milan. | | Non ho capito. | I did not understand. | | Ho due fratelli. | I have two brothers. | ### Register: formal vs informal The structure of a basic statement does not change much between formal and informal Italian. In formal situations, you may add Lei (the formal 'you') when speaking about the other person, but your own statements stay the same. ### Cultural note Italians often drop the subject pronoun because the verb ending already shows who is speaking. So Sono italiano is more natural than Io sono italiano, though both are correct. ### Common learner mistakes - **Keeping the subject pronoun**: Saying Io sono stanco is not wrong, but dropping io and saying Sono stanco sounds more natural. - **Using the wrong form of essere**: Remember sono = I am / they are; è = he/she/it is. Do not mix them up. - **Forgetting the article**: Say Sono uno studente, not Sono studente — Italian usually keeps the article in this pattern (though professions are an exception: Sono medico is also correct).

en.title: Describing people, places, and things
en.tip: Use è + adjective to say what something is like, e.g. Il libro è piccolo. Use c'è (there is) or ci sono (there are) to say what exists in a place.
en.why_this_matters: You will need to describe your room, your city, or a person almost every time you speak or write in Italian. This function lets you paint a picture with simple words from your very first lessons.
en.explanation: ## Describing people, places, and things This function lets you tell someone what a person, place, or object is like, or what is present somewhere. ### Key patterns **Pattern 1 — essere + adjective** Use the verb è (is) or sono (are) followed by an adjective: - La casa è grande. — The house is big. - Il gatto è nero. — The cat is black. - I bambini sono piccoli. — The children are small. Remember: Italian adjectives **agree** with the noun in gender and number. grande stays the same for masculine and feminine, but piccolo becomes piccola, piccoli, or piccole depending on the noun. **Pattern 2 — c'è / ci sono + noun phrase** Use c'è (there is) for one thing and ci sono (there are) for more than one: - C'è un supermercato vicino. — There is a supermarket nearby. - Ci sono due sedie in cucina. — There are two chairs in the kitchen. ### Register Both patterns work in formal and informal situations. In conversation you might shorten things: Bello! (Nice!) or Molto grande. (Very big.) — but full sentences are always safe. ### Cultural note Italians often add a short adjective after a noun for emphasis or warmth: una città bellissima (a very beautiful city). The suffix -issimo/a intensifies any adjective and is very common in everyday speech. ### Common learner mistakes - **Forgetting adjective agreement:** Saying la casa è grande ✓ but il gatto è negra ✗ — should be nero. - **Mixing up c'è and ci sono:** Use c'è for one item, ci sono for two or more. - **Omitting the article:** Say c'è un letto, not c'è letto.

en.title: Asking about a person or thing
en.tip: Use question words like chi (who), che cosa (what), or quale (which) to ask for information about people or objects. Add a verb and you have a complete question. Keep it simple at first!
en.why_this_matters: You will need this function constantly — in shops, at school, meeting new people, or just trying to understand the world around you in Italian. Being able to ask basic questions about people and things is one of the first real communication skills you build.
en.explanation: ## Asking about a person or thing This function is about forming questions to get information about **who** someone is or **what** something is. In Italian, you do this with interrogative sentences — sentences that ask rather than tell. ### Key question words | Italian | English | |---|---| | chi | who | | che cosa / cosa | what | | quale / quali | which / which ones | | com'è / come sono | what is … like / what are … like | ### Common patterns - Chi è? — *Who is it / who is he / who is she?* - Che cosa è questo? — *What is this?* - Cosa fai? — *What do you do / what are you doing?* - Che cosa mangi? — *What do you eat?* - Chi è quella persona? — *Who is that person?* - Qual è il tuo nome? — *What is your name?* ### Register: formal vs informal In everyday speech, Italians often shorten che cosa to just cosa: Cosa mangi? is perfectly natural and very common. The full form che cosa is slightly more careful or emphatic. Both are correct at all levels of formality. For **formal** situations (e.g. talking to a stranger or a professional), use the Lei form of the verb: Cosa fa Lei? (What do you do?). For **informal** situations with friends or peers, use tu: Cosa fai? ### Cultural note Italians are often warm and curious — asking questions about a person is seen as friendly interest, not intrusion, especially in casual settings. However, questions about age, money, or weight may feel personal, so use them carefully even in Italian. ### Common learner mistakes - **Forgetting the verb**: Cosa questo? ✗ → Cosa è questo? / Cos'è questo? ✓ - **Using che alone instead of che cosa**: Che mangi? is understood but sounds incomplete — prefer Cosa mangi? or Che cosa mangi? - **Wrong word order**: Italian questions often keep the same word order as statements — you raise your voice or use a question word instead of inverting subject and verb the way English does.

en.title: Asking about time
en.tip: Use quando (when) or a che ora (at what time) to ask when something happens. These two question words cover most situations where you need time information.
en.why_this_matters: You will need this every day — to catch a bus, find out when a shop opens, or arrange to meet someone. Knowing how to ask about time lets you navigate real life in Italy from day one.
en.explanation: ## Asking about time in Italian When you want to know **when** something happens or **at what time**, Italian gives you two main question words. ### Key question words | Italian | English | |---|---| | Quando? | When? | | A che ora? | At what time? | ### Patterns - **Quando** + verb → asks about a point in time (today, tomorrow, in summer, etc.) - **A che ora** + verb → asks for a specific clock time ### Example phrases - A che ora parte il treno per Roma? — *At what time does the train to Rome leave?* - Quando apre il museo? — *When does the museum open?* - A che ora inizia la lezione? — *At what time does the lesson start?* - Quando arriva Maria? — *When does Maria arrive?* ### Register (formal vs informal) These question words work in both formal and informal situations. The verb form changes, but quando and a che ora stay the same. - Informal: A che ora vieni? — *What time are you coming?* - Formal: A che ora arriva il direttore? — *At what time does the director arrive?* ### Common mistakes - **Using quando when you want a clock time.** If you need a specific hour, use a che ora. Quando parte il treno? is possible but might get a vague answer like *domani* (tomorrow). A che ora parte il treno? asks for the hour. - **Forgetting a before che ora.** Always say a che ora, not just che ora on its own in a question about when something happens.

label: Informarsi sul luogo

en.title: Asking where something is
en.tip: Use Dove (where) at the start of your question to ask about the location of a place, person, or thing. At A1 level, a simple Dove è...? or its contracted form Dov'è...? is all you need. Point or gesture freely — Italians appreciate the effort to communicate!
en.why_this_matters: You will need this function constantly when travelling, shopping, or exploring a new city. Being able to ask Dov'è la stazione? (Where is the station?) or Dove sono i bagni? (Where are the toilets?) can get you out of real trouble in everyday situations.
en.explanation: ## Asking about location Use this function when you want to find out **where** a person, place, or thing is. ### Key patterns | Italian | English | |---|---| | Dov'è...? | Where is...? | | Dove sono...? | Where are...? | | Dove si trova...? | Where is... located? | > **Note:** Dov'è is a contraction of dove è — the apostrophe replaces the final vowel of dove. Use it when the next word starts with a vowel sound. ### Examples - Dov'è Piazza Maggiore? — Where is Piazza Maggiore? - Dove sono i bagni? — Where are the toilets? - Dov'è il museo? — Where is the museum? - Dove si trova la farmacia? — Where is the pharmacy located? ### Formal vs informal Dov'è...? and Dove sono...? work in both formal and informal situations — no change needed. Dove si trova...? sounds slightly more formal or polite and is great when speaking to strangers or shop staff. ### Cultural note Italians are generally happy to help with directions. Starting with Scusi (Excuse me, formal) or Scusa (Excuse me, informal) before your question is polite and very common: Scusi, dov'è la stazione? ### Common mistakes - **Forgetting the apostrophe:** Write Dov'è, not Dove è — both are understood in speech, but the contraction is standard in writing. - **Using è for plural nouns:** Say Dove sono i bagni? (not Dov'è i bagni?) — use sono when asking about more than one thing. - **Skipping the article:** Italian usually requires a definite article — say Dov'è il supermercato?, not just Dov'è supermercato?

description: Ask 'how' questions to find out the way something is done or how someone is. Use Come ti chiami? or Come stai?.

en.title: Asking how something is done
en.tip: Use Come at the start of a question to ask about the way something happens or how someone feels. It is one of the most useful question words in Italian. You will hear and use it every day.
en.why_this_matters: Questions with Come let you learn someone's name, ask how they are, and find out how things work. These are among the very first questions you need when meeting people or navigating daily life in Italy.
en.explanation: ## Asking 'How' — Come...? ### What this function is for Use this function when you want to ask **how** something is done, how something is, or how someone is. The Italian question word is **come** (how). --- ### Key pattern | Pattern | English meaning | |---|---| | Come + verb + ...? | How + verb + ...? | --- ### Common phrases - **Come ti chiami?** — *What is your name?* (literally 'How do you call yourself?') - **Come si chiama?** — *What is your name?* (formal) / *What is it called?* - **Come stai?** — *How are you?* (informal) - **Come sta?** — *How are you?* (formal) - **Come si dice ... in italiano?** — *How do you say ... in Italian?* - **Come si scrive?** — *How do you write/spell it?* --- ### Formal vs informal Italian has two ways to say 'you': **tu** (informal, for friends and people you know well) and **Lei** (formal, for strangers, older people, or in professional settings). - Informal: Come **stai**? - Formal: Come **sta**? At A1, you mainly need both forms of stai/sta and ti chiami/si chiama. --- ### Cultural note In Italy, Come stai? / Come sta? is a genuine greeting. A short positive answer like Bene, grazie! (*Fine, thanks!*) is the normal reply — you do not need to go into detail. --- ### Common mistakes - **Mixing up come and cosa:** Come means *how*; cosa means *what*. Do not say ❌ Cosa ti chiami? — the correct form is ✅ Come ti chiami? - **Forgetting the verb:** In Italian the verb cannot be left out. Do not say ❌ Come tu? — always include the verb: ✅ Come stai? - **Using the wrong register:** With a teacher or a stranger, use the formal Come sta?, not the informal Come stai?

en.title: Asking about quantity or amount
en.tip: Use quanto (how much) or quanti/quante (how many) at the start of your question. The ending changes to match the noun — quanto, quanta, quanti, or quante. This one simple word lets you ask about prices, ages, distances, and counts.
en.why_this_matters: You will need this function the moment you go shopping, travel, or meet someone new in Italy. Knowing how to ask Quanto costa? or Quanti anni hai? immediately makes you a more confident, independent speaker.
en.explanation: ## Asking about quantity or amount Use this function whenever you want to find out **how much** or **how many** of something there is. ### Key pattern **Quanto / Quanta / Quanti / Quante + noun + verb?** The word quanto agrees in gender and number with the noun it refers to: | Form | Use with | Example | |------|----------|---------| | quanto | masculine singular | Quanto tempo? — How much time? | | quanta | feminine singular | Quanta acqua? — How much water? | | quanti | masculine plural | Quanti fratelli hai? — How many brothers do you have? | | quante | feminine plural | Quante persone? — How many people? | ### Common phrases - Quanto costa? — How much does it cost? - Quanto costano? — How much do they cost? - Quanti anni hai? — How old are you? (informal) - Quanti anni ha? — How old are you? (formal) - Quante ore ci vogliono? — How many hours does it take? ### Register: formal vs informal The quanto question works in both registers. To be formal, use the verb in the third-person singular (Lei form): - Informal: Quanti anni **hai**? - Formal: Quanti anni **ha**? ### Cultural note Asking Quanto costa? is completely natural in Italian shops, markets, and cafés. Italians expect customers to ask about prices directly — there is nothing rude about it. ### Common learner mistakes - **Using the wrong ending:** Saying *quanto persone* instead of quante persone. Always check the gender and number of the noun. - **Forgetting agreement when there is no noun:** When quanto stands alone (e.g. as the answer to 'how much did it cost?'), it stays as quanto for amounts: Quanto hai pagato? — How much did you pay? - **Confusing quanto with come:** Come means 'how' in the sense of manner (how do you do something), while quanto asks about degree or quantity.

en.title: Asking why — the reason for something
en.tip: Use Perché to ask for a reason or cause. It works on its own as a one-word question or at the start of a longer question. It is the same word whether you are speaking formally or informally.
en.why_this_matters: You will need this from day one — any time something surprises you or you do not understand why something is happening. It is one of the most common question words in everyday Italian conversation.
en.explanation: ## Asking about causes and reasons Use Perché (why) whenever you want to know the reason behind something. At A1 level, this is usually the word Perché? alone, or placed at the start of a simple question. ### Key patterns - Perché? — *Why?* (on its own, as a follow-up) - Perché + [subject] + [verb]? — *Why does/is [subject] [verb]?* - e.g. Perché sei triste? — *Why are you sad?* - e.g. Perché Marco non viene? — *Why isn't Marco coming?* - e.g. Perché il negozio è chiuso? — *Why is the shop closed?* ### Register Perché is neutral — it works in both formal and informal situations without any change. You do not need a different word depending on who you are speaking to. ### Important: two meanings of perché In Italian, perché means both *why* (in questions) and *because* (in answers). When someone answers your question, they will also use perché to give the reason: - Question: Perché sei in ritardo? — *Why are you late?* - Answer: Perché c'è traffico. — *Because there is traffic.* ### Common learner mistakes - **Using come mai too soon.** Come mai? also means *how come?* / *why?* and is common in informal speech, but stick with Perché at A1 level. - **Forgetting the accent.** Written as perché (with an accent on the final *e*). Without the accent it looks like the conjunction *because* — in writing, the accent is important. - **Confusing question and answer.** Remember that both the question (*why?*) and the answer (*because*) use the same word perché in Italian.

en.title: Asking 'Which one?' to identify
en.tip: Use quale (or qual before è) when you want someone to pick out or name a specific thing from a group. It works like 'which' or 'what' in English when you are identifying one item among several.
en.why_this_matters: You will need this any time you want to find out which specific thing someone means — a phone number, a name, a seat, a preference. It is one of the most common ways to ask for identifying information in everyday Italian life.
en.explanation: ## Asking 'Which one?' to identify Use this function when you want to ask someone to identify a specific person, thing, or option — not just describe it in general, but pick it out or name it. ### Key pattern The main word is quale, meaning 'which' or 'what (specific one)'. | Italian | English | |---|---| | Quale…? | Which…? | | Qual è…? | What/Which is…? | | Quali…? | Which ones…? (plural) | ### How it works - Before a noun: Quale autobus prendi? → 'Which bus do you take?' - With è (is): Qual è il tuo nome? → 'What is your name?' Note: quale drops the -e before è → qual è (no apostrophe). - Plural: Quali sono i tuoi libri? → 'Which ones are your books?' ### Register Quale / Qual è works in both formal and informal situations. You do not need to change the word — just adjust the rest of your sentence (tu vs Lei verb forms). - Informal: Qual è il tuo numero di telefono? - Formal: Qual è il Suo numero di telefono? ### Common learner mistakes - **Do not write qual'è with an apostrophe.** The correct form is qual è (two separate words, no apostrophe). This is one of the most common spelling errors in Italian. - **Do not confuse quale with che.** Both can mean 'what/which', but quale implies a choice among known options, while che is more open-ended. At A1 level, focus on quale for identification questions. - **Remember the plural quali** when asking about more than one thing: Quali lingue parli? → 'Which languages do you speak?'

en.title: Confirming or denying a statement
en.tip: Use simple words like sì, no, or certo to confirm something. To deny it, say no or non è vero. These short responses are enough at A1 level.
en.why_this_matters: You will constantly need to confirm or correct information in everyday life — when someone checks your name, address, or plans. Getting this right helps avoid misunderstandings from the very first conversations.
en.explanation: ## Confirming or Denying a Statement ### When to use this function Use this function when someone says something and you need to tell them whether it is **true or false** — for example, confirming your name, your nationality, or correcting a wrong assumption. --- ### Key phrases **To confirm:** | Italian | English | |---|---| | Sì | Yes | | Certo | Of course / Certainly | | È vero | That's true / That's right | | Sì, è vero | Yes, that's right | **To deny:** | Italian | English | |---|---| | No | No | | Non è vero | That's not true / That's wrong | | No, non è vero | No, that's not right | --- ### Examples in context - — Sei spagnolo? — No, sono italiano. — Are you Spanish? — No, I'm Italian. - — Abiti a Milano? — Sì, abito a Milano. — Do you live in Milan? — Yes, I live in Milan. - — È vero che parli inglese? — Certo! — Is it true that you speak English? — Of course! - — Questo è il tuo libro? — No, non è vero, non è mio. — Is this your book? — No, that's not right, it's not mine. --- ### Register: formal vs informal Sì and no work in **all situations** — formal and informal. Certo is slightly more emphatic and is used in both registers. Non è vero is a neutral, polite way to deny something without sounding rude. --- ### Common learner mistakes - **Forgetting non in negation:** To deny, you nearly always need non before the verb. Say non è vero, not just è non vero. - **Using sì to answer a negative question:** In Italian, if someone asks Non parli italiano? (Don't you speak Italian?) and you do speak Italian, you answer Sì, parlo italiano — just like in English ('Yes, I do'). This is straightforward at A1 level. - **Overcomplicating the answer:** At A1, a short Sì or No, non è vero is perfectly natural. You do not need a long explanation.

en.title: Answering yes or no
en.tip: When someone asks you a yes/no question, you can answer with a simple Sì (yes) or No (no). You can also confirm something is true with È vero or deny it with Non è vero.
en.why_this_matters: Yes/no questions come up constantly in everyday Italian — at a shop, in class, or when meeting new people. Knowing how to confirm or deny clearly lets you keep conversations moving even at beginner level.
en.explanation: ## Answering with a confirmation or denial When someone asks a yes/no question in Italian, you have several ways to respond. ### Basic yes and no | Italian | English | |---|---| | Sì | Yes | | No | No | | Certo | Of course / Certainly | **Examples:** - — Sei stanco? — Sì, sono stanco. — Are you tired? — Yes, I'm tired. - — Hai fame? — No, grazie. — Are you hungry? — No, thank you. - — Parli italiano? — Certo! — Do you speak Italian? — Of course! ### Confirming or denying a statement Use È vero (it's true) to confirm something, or Non è vero (it's not true) to deny it. - — È vero che sei di Milano? — Sì, è vero. — Is it true you're from Milan? — Yes, it's true. - — Non è vero che studi russo? — No, non è vero. — Isn't it true you study Russian? — No, it's not true. ### Register: formal vs informal Sì and No work in all situations — casual or formal. Certo is slightly more emphatic and can be used in both registers. In informal speech, Italians sometimes say sì, sì (repeated) for extra agreement. ### Common mistakes - Don't confuse sì (yes) with si (a reflexive pronoun). The accent makes a big difference in writing. - Avoid just saying vero alone as a full answer — always say È vero or Non è vero for clarity. - In Italian, double negatives are correct: No, non capisco (No, I don't understand) is normal and not a mistake.

en.title: Answering questions about time
en.tip: When someone asks you 'when?' or 'at what time?', reply with a time word or phrase like oggi (today), domani (tomorrow), or alle tre (at three o'clock). You can give a very short answer — just the time word on its own is perfectly natural.
en.why_this_matters: Italians ask about time all the time — meeting times, departure times, opening hours. Being able to answer quickly and clearly will make everyday conversations run smoothly from day one.
en.explanation: ## Answering questions about time When someone asks Quando? (When?) or A che ora? (At what time?), you need to give a time reference. At A1 level, this usually means using a single adverb or a prepositional phrase. ### Key patterns **Adverbs** — stand alone or at the start of a sentence: - oggi — today - domani — tomorrow - ieri — yesterday - adesso / ora — now - dopo — later / after - presto — soon / early - tardi — late **Prepositional phrases** — give a more specific time: - alle + time — at (a clock time): alle otto (at eight o'clock), alle tre e mezza (at half past three) - a + time — at (used with noon and midnight): a mezzogiorno (at noon) - di mattina / di sera / di notte — in the morning / in the evening / at night ### Short vs full answers In conversation, a one-word answer is completely natural: - *Quando parti?* — 'When are you leaving?' → Domani. ✓ - *A che ora inizia?* — 'What time does it start?' → Alle nove. ✓ You can also give a fuller answer: - Parto domani mattina. — I'm leaving tomorrow morning. - Il film inizia alle otto di sera. — The film starts at eight in the evening. ### Register: formal vs informal Time expressions themselves do not change between formal and informal registers. What changes is the surrounding sentence. In a formal context you might say Il treno parte alle 10.00. In an informal context Parto alle dieci! is fine. ### Common mistakes - **Confusing alle and a**: Use alle for numbered hours (alle due, alle sette) and a only for mezzogiorno and mezzanotte. - **Forgetting alle entirely**: Saying just otto instead of alle otto sounds incomplete. Always include the preposition when giving a clock time. - **Word order**: Time adverbs like oggi and domani can go at the beginning or end of a sentence — both are correct.

en.title: Answering questions about location
en.tip: When someone asks 'where?', reply with a simple location word or short phrase. Even a single word like lì (there) works perfectly at this level. You can point or gesture to help make your meaning clear.
en.why_this_matters: People ask 'where' questions all the time — where is the station, the bathroom, the school? Being able to give a short, clear location answer lets you communicate in shops, streets, and everyday situations from day one.
en.explanation: ## Answering 'Where?' Questions When someone asks Dov'è…? (Where is…?) or Dove…? (Where…?), you can answer with a location adverb or a short phrase. ### Key Words and Patterns **Single adverbs (often with a gesture):** - Qui — Here - Qua — Here (slightly more informal variant) - Lì — There - Là — There (a little further away) - Su — Up / Upstairs - Giù — Down / Downstairs - Dentro — Inside - Fuori — Outside - Vicino — Nearby - Lontano — Far away **Short phrases with** è **(is) or** sono **(are):** - È lì. — It's there. - È qui. — It's here. - È in centro. — It's in the centre. - È vicino alla stazione. — It's near the station. - È al primo piano. — It's on the first floor. - È a sinistra / a destra. — It's on the left / on the right. - È dritto. — It's straight ahead. ### Register Location answers are mostly the same in both formal and informal situations. A single adverb (lì) is fine with friends; in a more formal context you might add È at the start: È lì, signora. ### Cultural Note Italians frequently combine spoken answers with hand gestures — pointing, waving a hand to indicate direction. At A1 level this is not just acceptable, it is very natural and helpful. ### Common Learner Mistakes - **Confusing lì and là:** Both mean 'there', but là often suggests something slightly further away. At A1, either is understood. - **Forgetting è:** Saying just stazione instead of È in stazione can sound incomplete. A bare adverb (lì) is fine, but a noun answer needs the verb. - **Using direction words without prepositions:** Say a sinistra (on the left), not just sinistra alone.

en.title: Answering questions about manner
en.tip: When someone asks Come? (How?), reply with a simple adverb like bene (well) or male (badly). You can add grazie to sound polite. Keep it short — one adverb is enough at this level.
en.why_this_matters: Questions like Come stai? (How are you?) and Come va? (How's it going?) come up in every conversation. Knowing how to answer naturally with the right adverb will make your Italian sound fluent from day one.
en.explanation: ## Answering questions about manner When someone asks Come? (How?) or Come stai? (How are you?), they want to know **how** something is happening or how you feel. At A1, you answer with a simple **adverb of manner**. ### Key phrases | Italian | English | |---|---| | Bene, grazie. | Well, thanks. | | Male. | Badly. | | Abbastanza bene. | Quite well. | | Non c'è male. | Not bad. | | Così così. | So-so. | | Lentamente. | Slowly. | | Velocemente. | Quickly. | ### How it works In Italian, adverbs of manner are often formed by adding -mente to an adjective, similar to English '-ly'. For example, lento → lentamente (slow → slowly). However, at A1 level the most useful adverbs are short, common words like bene and male that you simply need to memorise. ### Register: formal vs informal Adverbs themselves do not change between formal and informal speech. However, the question you are answering may vary: - Informal: Come stai? → Bene, grazie! - Formal: Come sta? → Bene, grazie. The answer is the same — only the question form changes. ### Cultural note Italians often add a brief follow-up like E tu? (And you?) or E Lei? (formal) after answering. This shows politeness and keeps the conversation going. ### Common mistakes - **Using an adjective instead of an adverb.** In Italian, you must say Sto bene (I am well), not Sto buono. Buono is an adjective meaning 'good' (for things or food), while bene is the adverb used with verbs like stare. - **Forgetting to add grazie.** While not required, omitting it can sound abrupt. It is a small word that makes a big difference in tone.

en.title: Answering questions about degree and quantity
en.tip: Use an adverb like molto or poco to answer 'how much / how well' questions. Use a number or quantity word to answer 'how many' questions. Keep it short — one word is often enough.
en.why_this_matters: People will ask you how you are, how much something costs, or how many of something you want every day. Knowing how to give a quick, clear answer to these questions will make your conversations flow naturally from the very start.
en.explanation: ## Answering questions about degree and quantity This function covers how to reply when someone asks about **how much**, **how many**, or **to what degree** something is true. ### When to use this function Use it to respond to questions like: - Come va? (How are you / How is it going?) - Quanti anni hai? (How old are you?) - Quanto costa? (How much does it cost?) - Quante persone ci sono? (How many people are there?) ### Key patterns **Adverbs of degree** — answer 'how much' or 'how well': | Italian | English | |---|---| | molto bene | very well | | abbastanza bene | quite well | | poco | a little / not much | | molto | a lot / very | | troppo | too much | **Numbers and quantity words** — answer 'how many': | Italian | English | |---|---| | venticinque | twenty-five | | due | two | | molti / molte | many | | pochi / poche | few | | tanti / tante | lots of | ### Register: formal vs informal These answers work in both formal and informal situations. In a formal context you might add a full sentence, but a short answer is always acceptable: - Informal: — Come stai? — Bene, grazie! - More formal: — Come sta? — Molto bene, grazie. ### Common learner mistakes - **Confusing molto as an adverb and adjective.** As an adverb it never changes: sto molto bene. As an adjective before a noun it must agree: molti libri, molte persone. - **Forgetting bene after molto for 'very well'.** Don't say molto buono when describing how you feel — say molto bene. - **Using buono instead of bene.** Bene is an adverb (modifies a verb), while buono is an adjective (describes a noun).

en.title: Answering 'why' questions with a reason
en.tip: When someone asks Perché...? (Why...?), answer with Perché followed by a verb phrase giving your reason. The same word perché means both 'why' and 'because' in Italian.
en.why_this_matters: People ask 'why' all the time — why you are leaving, why you are tired, why you are late. Being able to give a simple reason helps you have real conversations from your very first days of learning Italian.
en.explanation: ## Answering 'why' questions with a reason When someone asks you Perché...? (Why...?), you answer with Perché + a verb phrase explaining the cause or reason. ### The key pattern **Perché + verb phrase** Examples: - Perché sono stanco. — Because I'm tired. - Perché ho fame. — Because I'm hungry. - Perché devo lavorare. — Because I have to work. ### How the question and answer work together | Question | Answer | |---|---| | Perché vai a casa? (Why are you going home?) | Perché sono stanco. (Because I'm tired.) | | Perché non mangi? (Why aren't you eating?) | Perché non ho fame. (Because I'm not hungry.) | | Perché studi l'italiano? (Why do you study Italian?) | Perché voglio andare in Italia. (Because I want to go to Italy.) | ### The same word for 'why' and 'because' In Italian, perché does double duty — it means **why** (in questions) and **because** (in answers). This is different from English, where they are two separate words. Don't let this confuse you: just remember that when perché starts your answer, it means 'because'. ### Register This pattern works in both formal and informal situations. You do not need to change the word perché depending on who you are speaking to. ### Common learner mistakes - **Using two different words:** English learners sometimes try to say ~~per~~ or ~~poiché~~ when they mean 'because' in simple everyday replies. At A1 level, perché is the right and natural choice. - **Forgetting the verb:** Do not just say ~~Perché stanco.~~ — you need the verb: Perché sono stanco. - **Capitalising:** Perché is only capitalised at the start of a sentence, just like in English.

en.title: Identifying a person or thing
en.tip: When someone asks 'who is that?' or 'which one do you want?', point and say questo or quello, or use è plus a noun to name someone or something. To give a name, say si chiama followed by the name.
en.why_this_matters: People will ask you to point out objects, name people, or identify things around you from your very first days of speaking Italian. These short answers let you respond clearly and naturally, even with a very small vocabulary.
en.explanation: ## Answering by identifying When someone asks a question like 'Chi è?' (Who is it?), 'Quale vuoi?' (Which one do you want?), or 'Come si chiama?' (What is his/her name?), you can answer by identifying the person or thing. ### Key patterns **1. Point to something: questo / quello** Use questo (this / this one) for something close to you, and quello (that / that one) for something further away. These change ending depending on gender: | | Masculine | Feminine | |---|---|---| | near | questo | questa | | far | quello | quella | At A1, a gesture (pointing) often goes with these words. Example: - Vorrei questo. — I would like this one. - Quella, per favore. — That one, please. **2. Name or describe with è + noun phrase** Use è (is) plus a noun to identify who or what something is: - È la mia professoressa. — She is my teacher. - È un cane. — It's a dog. - È Marco, il mio amico. — It's Marco, my friend. **3. Give a name with si chiama + name** Use si chiama (his/her name is, literally 'he/she is called') to identify someone by name: - Si chiama Giulia. — Her name is Giulia. - Lui si chiama Mario. — His name is Mario. For your own name, use mi chiamo: - Mi chiamo Anna. — My name is Anna. ### Register (formal vs informal) All three patterns work in both formal and informal situations. In a shop or with a stranger, pointing with questo / quello plus per favore is perfectly polite. With friends, you can drop per favore. ### Common mistakes - **Forgetting gender agreement:** questo must match the noun — questo libro (masculine) but questa borsa (feminine). At A1, keep it simple: if you are not sure, pointing plus questo is understood. - **Confusing è and ha:** Use è to identify ('is'), not ha ('has'). Say È il mio professore, not Ha il mio professore. - **Mixing up mi chiamo and si chiama:** Mi chiamo is for yourself; si chiama is for someone else.

en.title: Saying you don't know
en.tip: When someone asks you a question and you don't have the answer, simply say Non lo so or Non so. Both mean 'I don't know' and are perfectly natural in Italian. You can add mi dispiace ('I'm sorry') to sound more polite.
en.why_this_matters: Even at beginner level, people will ask you questions you can't answer. Knowing how to say 'I don't know' clearly and naturally helps you stay in the conversation without freezing up. It's one of the most frequently used phrases in everyday Italian.
en.explanation: ## Saying You Don't Know Sometimes the most important thing you can say is that you don't have an answer. In Italian, there are two closely related phrases for this: ### Key Phrases | Italian | English | |---|---| | Non lo so | I don't know (it) | | Non so | I don't know | Both are correct and very common. Non lo so is slightly more emphatic — the lo ('it') refers back to the specific thing being asked about. Non so is used more as a general 'I don't know', often before a clause (e.g. Non so perché... — 'I don't know why...'). ### Making It More Polite You can soften the response by adding: - Non lo so, mi dispiace. — 'I don't know, I'm sorry.' - Non lo so, scusa. — 'I don't know, sorry.' (informal) ### Register Both Non lo so and Non so work equally well in formal and informal situations. They are neutral, everyday phrases. ### Cultural Note Italians often pair Non lo so with a shrug or an upward palm gesture — don't be surprised if you see this! It's a common non-verbal companion to the phrase. ### Common Mistakes - **Don't say** Non so lo — the word order is wrong. The pronoun lo always comes directly before the verb: Non **lo** so. - **Don't confuse** Non so (I don't know) with Non sono (I am not). They sound similar but mean very different things.

en.title: Agreeing without reservation
en.tip: When someone says something and you fully agree, a simple Sì is all you need in Italian. It is direct, clear, and natural. You can say it on its own or pair it with a short phrase to sound more engaged.
en.why_this_matters: Agreement is one of the most basic moves in any conversation — you will use it every day from your very first interactions in Italian. Knowing how to signal full agreement quickly keeps the conversation flowing and shows you are listening.
en.explanation: ## Agreeing Without Reservation This function is about signalling that you completely share what another person has said — no doubt, no hesitation, no 'but'. ### When to use it Use this when someone makes a statement and you want to confirm you agree entirely. It can follow a comment about the weather, a situation, an opinion, or any simple observation. ### Key phrase | Italian | English | |---|---| | Sì | Yes / That's right | At A1, Sì is the core pattern. It works in almost any context and with almost any statement. ### How it works in context Agreement usually follows a statement made by someone else: - A: Fa caldo oggi. ('It's hot today.') - B: Sì. ('Yes.' / 'You're right.') - A: Il caffè è buono. ('The coffee is good.') - B: Sì! ('Yes, it is!') ### Register: formal vs informal Sì works in both formal and informal situations. It is never rude or too casual. In more informal speech, Italians sometimes repeat it — Sì, sì — to sound warmer and more enthusiastic, though a single Sì is always correct. ### Cultural note Italians tend to be expressive, so how you say Sì matters as much as the word itself. A warm tone and a nod make your agreement feel natural and genuine. ### Common learner mistakes - **Confusing sì (yes) with si (reflexive pronoun):** In writing, sì always carries an accent mark. In speech this is not an issue, but be careful in written exercises. - **Overcomplicating it:** Beginners sometimes search for a longer phrase when a simple Sì is exactly right. Trust it — it is a complete, natural answer.

en.title: Disagreeing with a positive statement
en.tip: To disagree with something someone has said, simply say No, and then give the correct information. You don't need complex phrases — a short, clear correction is enough at this level.
en.why_this_matters: You will often hear things that are wrong — about the weather, a place, a person, or a fact. Being able to politely but clearly say 'no, that's not right' is one of the most basic conversation skills you need from day one.
en.explanation: ## Disagreeing with a Positive Statement This function lets you push back when someone says something you think is incorrect. At A1, the pattern is simple: **Pattern:** No, + correct statement ### Key Phrases | Italian | English | |---|---| | No, fa caldo. | No, it's hot. | | No, è lontano. | No, it's far. | | No, lei si chiama Anna. | No, her name is Anna. | | No, il negozio è chiuso. | No, the shop is closed. | ### How It Works The structure is very straightforward. Someone makes a positive claim, and you respond with No, followed by the statement you believe to be true. - Someone says: "Fa freddo oggi." (It's cold today.) - You reply: "No, fa caldo!" (No, it's hot!) ### Register This pattern works in both formal and informal situations. Tone of voice matters more than the words themselves — say No calmly to sound polite, not confrontational. ### Cultural Note Italians often express disagreement quite directly and with energy. A firm No is normal and not considered rude as long as your tone is friendly. ### Common Learner Mistakes - **Leaving out the correction:** Saying just No can sound abrupt or unclear. Always follow it with the correct information. - **Overcomplicating it:** At A1, you don't need phrases like Non sono d'accordo (I disagree) — a simple No, + correction is perfect.

en.title: Saying 'Good!' to show approval
en.tip: Use Bene! to show you approve of something — it means 'Good!' or 'Well done!' in English. You can say it on its own or combine it with other words like Molto bene! (Very good!) to sound more enthusiastic.
en.why_this_matters: Showing approval is something you will do every day — responding to news, reacting to what someone has done, or simply encouraging a friend. Even one short word like Bene! goes a long way in making a conversation feel natural and warm.
en.explanation: ## Expressing approval in Italian When you want to say that something is good, correct, or well done, Italian uses a small set of simple exclamations that are easy to learn and use right away. ### Key phrases | Italian | English | |---|---| | Bene! | Good! / Well done! | | Molto bene! | Very good! | | Benissimo! | Excellent! / Very well! | | Perfetto! | Perfect! | | Bravo! / Brava! | Well done! (to a male / female) | ### When to use this function Use these words when someone tells you good news, shows you something they have done, or completes a task. For example: - Someone says Ho finito il lavoro (I finished the work) → you reply Bene! - A child reads correctly → you say Bravo! - A friend books the restaurant → you say Perfetto! ### Register: formal vs informal Bene! works in both formal and informal situations — it is neutral and safe to use with anyone. Bravo / Brava is slightly more personal and warm, often used with children or friends, but it is also common in everyday adult conversation. Perfetto! is polite and works well in service situations such as shops and restaurants. ### Cultural note Italians often use these words with expressive tone and body language. A simple Bene! said with a nod and a smile communicates a lot. Do not worry about saying too little — short, warm responses are completely normal. ### Common learner mistakes - Do not confuse Bene! (approval / good) with Buono / Buona (tasty / good quality). Bene is an adverb used to react to actions or situations, not to describe food or objects. - Remember that Bravo changes to Brava for a woman, Bravi for a group.

description: Express that you know something or someone. Use phrases like Lo so or Conosco... to share your knowledge in conversation.

en.title: Saying what you know
en.tip: Use so (from sapere) to say you know a fact or piece of information. Use conosco (from conoscere) to say you know a person or place. Both mean 'I know', but they are used differently.
en.why_this_matters: Telling someone you already know something is a very common part of everyday conversation. At A1 level, even a simple Lo so! shows you are following along and engaging with the speaker.
en.explanation: ## Saying what you know In Italian, there are two verbs for 'to know', and choosing the right one depends on *what* you know. ### Sapere — knowing facts or information Use sapere when you know a fact, a piece of information, or how to do something. | Italian | English | |---|---| | Lo so. | I know (it). | | So dove abita. | I know where she lives. | | So parlare italiano. | I know how to speak Italian. | | So già la risposta. | I already know the answer. | The word lo in Lo so means 'it' and refers to the piece of information. This is the most common short answer. ### Conoscere — knowing a person or place Use conoscere when you know a person, a place, or something you are familiar with through experience. | Italian | English | |---|---| | Conosco Maria. | I know Maria. | | Conosco bene Roma. | I know Rome well. | | Conosco questo ristorante. | I know this restaurant. | ### Register Both Lo so and Conosco... work in both formal and informal situations. They are neutral and natural in any context. ### Common mistakes - Do not use conosco for facts. Saying *Conosco dove abita is wrong. Use So dove abita. - Do not forget lo when replying to a question about information. Lo so is much more natural than just So alone. - English speakers sometimes use only one verb for both meanings, but in Italian the distinction between sapere and conoscere is important from the very beginning.

en.title: Saying you don't know something
en.tip: Use Non lo so whenever you cannot answer a question. It is a fixed, ready-made phrase — you do not need to change any part of it at this level. A shrug or a filler like mah can make it sound more natural.
en.why_this_matters: You will often be asked questions you simply cannot answer — about directions, prices, or facts. Knowing how to say 'I don't know' politely lets you respond honestly without feeling stuck or embarrassed.
en.explanation: ## Expressing That You Don't Know At A1 level, there is one key phrase for this function: | Italian | English | |---|---| | Non lo so. | I don't know. | ### When to use it Use Non lo so when someone asks you a question and you genuinely cannot give the answer. It works in almost any situation — on the street, in class, at a shop, or on the phone. ### How it works Non lo so is best treated as a **fixed formula** at this level. Literally it means 'I don't know it', where lo stands for the piece of information being asked about. You do not need to change the phrase — just say it as it is. ### Making it sound more natural Adding a filler or a short extra phrase makes your response feel warmer and more fluent: - Mah, non lo so. — *Well, I don't know.* (shows you are thinking) - Non lo so, mi dispiace. — *I don't know, I'm sorry.* - Non lo so, sorry! — casual, mixing in an English loanword sometimes heard among younger speakers. ### Register Non lo so is neutral — it fits both formal and informal situations. There is no special polite or rude version at this level. ### Cultural note Italians often accompany non lo so with a slight shrug or raised hands. This is completely normal and makes the phrase feel natural rather than abrupt. ### Common learner mistakes - **Saying non so alone** — Non so exists in Italian but has a slightly different feel and is less common in everyday reply situations. Stick with Non lo so. - **Translating word-for-word from English** and producing something like *Io non conosco* — this is not the right phrase here. Conoscere is for knowing people or places, not for knowing a piece of information.

en.title: Saying what you can or can't do
en.tip: Use so (from the verb sapere) followed by an infinitive to say you know how to do something. To say you can't, just add non before so. This is the most natural way at A1 to talk about your abilities.
en.why_this_matters: You'll need this from your very first Italian conversations — introducing yourself, answering questions about your hobbies, or explaining what help you can offer. It's a simple pattern you can use immediately with any verb you already know.
en.explanation: ## Expressing ability and inability Use this function when you want to tell someone what you **can** or **cannot** do — a skill, a talent, or a learned ability. ### Key pattern | Italian | English | |---|---| | So + infinitive | I can / I know how to + verb | | Non so + infinitive | I can't / I don't know how to + verb | ### Examples - So scrivere. — I can write. - So parlare italiano. — I can speak Italian. - Non so cucinare. — I can't cook. - So suonare la chitarra. — I can play the guitar. - Non so nuotare. — I can't swim. ### The verb sapere The form so is the first-person singular of sapere (to know). When followed by an infinitive, sapere expresses **knowing how** to do something — a learned skill or ability. > **Note:** Italian also uses potere (can, to be able to) for ability, but sapere + infinitive is the most common and natural choice at A1 when talking about personal skills. ### Register This pattern works in **both formal and informal** situations. There is no register difference — you can say So guidare to a friend or in a job interview. ### Common learner mistakes - **Using posso instead of so:** English speakers often translate 'I can cook' as Posso cucinare, but this means 'I am allowed to cook' or 'I am able to cook right now'. For a general skill, use So cucinare. - **Forgetting the infinitive:** Always follow so with the base form of the verb — e.g. So ballare, not So ballo.

en.title: Expressing a wish or desire
en.tip: Use vorrei followed by a noun to say what you want. It is polite and works in almost any situation. Think of it as the Italian way of saying 'I would like'.
en.why_this_matters: You will need this function the moment you walk into a café, shop, or restaurant in Italy. It is one of the most useful phrases you can learn at beginner level, and using it shows good manners right away.
en.explanation: ## Expressing a Wish or Desire ### What this function is for Use this function when you want to tell someone what you would like — in a shop, a bar, a restaurant, or any everyday situation. ### Key pattern | Pattern | English | |---|---| | Vorrei + [noun] | I would like + [thing] | Vorrei is the conditional form of volere (to want). You do not need to understand all of Italian grammar to use it — just remember it as a fixed, polite phrase. ### Examples - Vorrei un caffè. — I would like a coffee. - Vorrei un biglietto, per favore. — I would like a ticket, please. - Vorrei una camera singola. — I would like a single room. - Vorrei dell'acqua. — I would like some water. ### Register: formal and informal Vorrei is naturally polite and works in both formal and informal contexts. You can say it to a waiter, a shopkeeper, or a friend. Adding per favore (please) makes it even more courteous. Avoid using voglio (I want) in service situations — it can sound too blunt or even rude to Italian ears, especially with strangers. ### Cultural note In Italy, ordering at a bar or café is very common. Saying Vorrei un caffè, per favore as you approach the counter is perfectly natural and will immediately make a good impression. ### Common mistakes - **Using voglio instead of vorrei**: Voglio un caffè is grammatically correct but sounds abrupt. Stick with vorrei when talking to people you do not know well. - **Forgetting the article**: Say Vorrei **un** caffè, not Vorrei caffè. Italian nouns almost always need an article.

en.title: Expressing an intention
en.tip: To say what you plan to do, use voglio (I want / I intend to) followed by a verb in the infinitive. It is simple, direct, and works in almost any situation at this level.
en.why_this_matters: You will need this function whenever you talk about your plans — booking a trip, starting a new hobby, or explaining a decision. It is one of the most common ways Italian speakers express future intentions in everyday conversation.
en.explanation: ## Expressing an intention in Italian ### What this function is for Use this function when you want to tell someone what you plan, intend, or have decided to do. ### Key pattern | Pattern | English | |---|---| | Voglio + infinitive | I want to / I intend to + verb | **Examples:** - Voglio cambiare casa. — I want to move house. - Voglio studiare italiano. — I want to study Italian. - Voglio comprare un biglietto. — I want to buy a ticket. - Voglio parlare con il direttore. — I want to speak to the manager. ### Register: formal vs informal Voglio is perfectly natural in both informal and moderately formal contexts. In very formal situations (for example, a written request), Italians might prefer vorrei (I would like to), which sounds more polite. At A1 level, voglio is the core form to learn first. ### Cultural note Italians often use voglio freely in conversation — it does not sound rude the way 'I want' can sometimes feel in English. Even so, adding per favore (please) softens any request made to a stranger or in a service context. ### Common learner mistakes - **Using a conjugated verb instead of the infinitive:** ✗ Voglio studio italiano. ✓ Voglio studiare italiano. - **Confusing intention with desire:** Voglio covers both 'I want' and 'I intend to' in Italian, so there is no need to search for a separate word for 'intend'. - **Forgetting that the infinitive does not change:** Voglio mangiare, voglio dormire, voglio partire — the infinitive form always ends in -are, -ere, or -ire and stays the same regardless of subject.

en.title: Expressing obligation and prohibition
en.tip: Use devo (I must / I have to) followed by an infinitive verb to say what you are obliged to do. To say something is forbidden, use non si può (you can't / it's not allowed) or è vietato (it's forbidden).
en.why_this_matters: You'll need these phrases constantly in everyday life — telling someone you have to leave, explaining a rule at school or work, or reading a sign that prohibits something. Getting this right helps you sound natural and avoid misunderstandings about what is required or not allowed.
en.explanation: ## Expressing Obligation and Prohibition ### When to use this function Use this function when you want to say that you — or someone else — **must do something** (obligation) or **must not do something** (prohibition). This comes up in daily life: schedules, rules, signs, and social duties. --- ### Key phrases and patterns #### Obligation — saying what you must do | Italian | English | |---|---| | Devo studiare. | I have to study. | | Devo andare a lezione. | I have to go to class. | | Devi aspettare qui. | You have to wait here. | | Deve parlare con il professore. | He/She has to speak with the teacher. | The pattern is: **dovere** (conjugated) + infinitive verb. | Subject | dovere | |---|---| | io | devo | | tu | devi | | lui / lei | deve | #### Prohibition — saying what is not allowed | Italian | English | |---|---| | Non si può fumare qui. | You can't smoke here. | | È vietato entrare. | Entry is forbidden. | | Non puoi parcheggiare qui. | You can't park here. | Non si può + infinitive is very common on signs and in spoken rules. È vietato + infinitive is more formal and often written. --- ### Register: formal vs informal - With friends or family, devo and devi are perfectly natural. - In formal or written contexts (rules, signs, official notices), prefer è vietato or non è consentito (not permitted). --- ### Cultural note In Italy, public signs often use vietato — for example, Vietato fumare (No smoking) or Vietato l'accesso (No entry). Knowing these fixed phrases helps you navigate public spaces confidently. --- ### Common learner mistakes - ❌ Devo andare a lezione domani with the future tense after devo — remember, dovere is always followed by an **infinitive**, not a conjugated verb. - ❌ Saying ho da fare when you mean devo fare — while ho da fare exists in Italian, it means 'I'm busy', not a direct obligation. - ✅ Keep it simple at A1: devo + infinitive covers most situations perfectly.

en.title: Apologizing in Italian
en.tip: Use Scusi with people you don't know well or in formal situations, and Scusa with friends or family. Both words cover 'sorry' and 'excuse me' in everyday use.
en.why_this_matters: You will need this word constantly — when you bump into someone, arrive late, or make a small mistake. Getting Scusi vs Scusa right shows respect and good manners from day one.
en.explanation: ## Apologizing: Scusi / Scusa ### When to use this function Use Scusi or Scusa whenever you want to: - apologize for a small mistake or inconvenience - politely interrupt someone - get a stranger's attention before asking a question ### Key phrases | Italian | English | |---|---| | Scusi | Sorry / Excuse me (formal) | | Scusa | Sorry / Excuse me (informal) | ### Formal vs informal - **Formal** — use Scusi with strangers, older people, teachers, shop assistants, or anyone you address as Lei. - **Informal** — use Scusa with friends, classmates, or family members. ### How these words work Both Scusi and Scusa come from the verb scusare (to excuse). At A1 level you do not need to analyze the grammar — treat them as fixed, ready-to-use phrases. ### Cultural note In Italy, Scusi is extremely common in public spaces — on the bus, in a shop, in a corridor. Using it freely is a sign of politeness, not weakness. Italians also use it to soften a request: Scusi, dov'è il bagno? ('Excuse me, where is the bathroom?'). ### Common learner mistakes - **Mixing up formal and informal.** Saying Scusa to a professor or elderly stranger can sound rude. When in doubt, use Scusi. - **Forgetting to use it.** English speakers sometimes skip the apology and go straight to the question. In Italian, adding Scusi first sounds much more natural and polite.

en.title: Expressing happiness and joy
en.tip: Use simple phrases like Sono felice or Che bello! to share good feelings. You can add molto (very) to make your emotion stronger. These phrases work in most everyday situations.
en.why_this_matters: Reacting to good news, sharing excitement, and showing happiness are things you will do constantly in Italian — with friends, family, and even strangers. Learning to express joy naturally makes conversations feel warm and real from the very beginning.
en.explanation: ## Expressing Happiness and Joy This function lets you tell people you are happy, excited, or pleased. At A1 level, a small set of phrases covers most situations. ### Key phrases | Italian | English | |---|---| | Sono felice | I am happy | | Sono contento / contenta | I am happy / pleased | | Che bello! | How great! / How lovely! | | Che gioia! | What joy! | | Evviva! | Hurray! | | Sono molto felice | I am very happy | ### Adding more detail You can say what you are happy *about* using di + infinitive or di + noun: - Sono felice di vederti. — I am happy to see you. - Sono contento del regalo. — I am happy about the gift. ### Register These phrases work in both formal and informal situations. Exclamations like Che bello! and Evviva! are more common in informal, spontaneous speech. In more formal contexts, Sono molto contento/a sounds natural and polished. ### Cultural note Italians often express emotions openly and with enthusiasm. A warm exclamation like Che gioia! or Che bello! is perfectly normal and will be well received in social settings. ### Common mistakes - Remember that contento and felice are adjectives — they must agree with the speaker's gender: contento (male) / contenta (female). Felice stays the same for both genders. - Do not say Sono molto contento di followed by a conjugated verb. Use the infinitive instead: Sono contento di venire, not ~~Sono contento di vengo~~.

en.title: Expressing Sadness or Longing
en.tip: Use simple phrases with 'sono' (I am) or 'non sto bene' (I'm not well) to share that you feel sad. To say you miss someone or something, use 'mi manca' followed by the person or place.
en.why_this_matters: Being able to say how you feel is essential in everyday conversation. Whether you're having a bad day or missing home, these phrases help people around you understand your emotions and respond with kindness.
en.explanation: ## Expressing Sadness or Longing This function lets you tell someone that you are sad, unwell emotionally, or that you miss a person or place. At A1 level, a few simple phrases go a long way. ### Key Phrases | Italian | English | |---|---| | Non sto bene. | I'm not well. / I'm not doing well. | | Sono triste. | I am sad. | | Sono molto triste. | I am very sad. | | Mi manca [persona/luogo]. | I miss [person/place]. | | Mi sento solo / sola. | I feel lonely. | | Ho nostalgia di casa. | I feel homesick. | ### How to Use These Phrases **Saying you are sad:** The easiest way is Sono triste — just like saying 'I am sad' in English. You can add molto (very) to make it stronger: Sono molto triste. **Saying you don't feel well emotionally:** Non sto bene literally means 'I am not well' and can refer to feeling sad or unwell in general. It is softer than saying sono triste directly. **Saying you miss someone or something:** In Italian, 'I miss my mum' is expressed differently from English. You say Mi manca mia mamma — literally 'My mum is missing to me.' The verb is mancare and it works like the verb 'piacere'. - Mi manca Roma. — I miss Rome. - Mi mancano i miei amici. — I miss my friends. (plural: mancano) **Saying you feel homesick:** Ho nostalgia di casa is a very natural Italian expression. Nostalgia exists in English too, but in Italian it is used for everyday homesickness as well as deeper longing. ### Register: Formal vs Informal These phrases work in both formal and informal situations. With friends or family, you might say Sto male, mi manca tanto la mia famiglia. In a more formal context, such as talking to a doctor or teacher, Non sto bene or Mi sento un po' giù (I feel a bit down) are appropriate. ### Cultural Note Italians are generally expressive about emotions, and sharing feelings with friends or family is perfectly normal. Saying Mi manchi (I miss you) to a friend or partner is common and warm, not overly dramatic. ### Common Learner Mistakes - **'Mi manca' vs 'manco':** Do not say Io manco la mia famiglia. The correct structure is Mi manca la mia famiglia — the thing or person missed is the subject. - **Singular vs plural:** Mi manca (one thing/person) vs Mi mancano (more than one). Many learners forget to change the verb for plurals. - **'Non sto bene' vs 'non sono bene':** Always use stare for temporary states: non sto bene, not non sono bene.

en.title: Asking how someone feels

en.why_this_matters: Asking how someone feels is one of the first things you do when you meet a person in Italian. It shows you care and helps you start a natural conversation.
en.explanation: ## Asking About Someone's Feelings This function lets you check in on how someone is feeling — whether they are happy, sad, or somewhere in between. ### Key Phrases | Italian | English | |---|---| | Come stai? | How are you? (informal) | | Come sta? | How are you? (formal) | | Tutto bene? | Everything OK? | | Sei felice? | Are you happy? | | Sei triste? | Are you sad? | | Come ti senti? | How do you feel? (informal) | ### Formal vs Informal - Use Come stai? and Come ti senti? with friends, family, and children. - Use Come sta? with teachers, shop staff, or anyone you address as Lei. - Tutto bene? works in both contexts and is very common in everyday Italian. ### Cultural Note In Italy, Come stai? is often a social greeting rather than a deep question. A simple Bene, grazie! ('Fine, thanks!') is the expected reply in most casual situations. If you notice someone looks upset, adding Sembri un po' triste ('You look a little sad') shows warmth and attention. ### Common Mistakes - Do not use Come stai? when speaking formally — switch to Come sta? - Do not confuse Come stai? (How are you?) with Come sei? (What are you like? / What do you look like?) — they mean very different things.

en.why_this_matters: Knowing how to express fear or distress is essential for safety situations — for example, when you are lost, scared, or need help. Even a single word like Aiuto! can make a real difference.
en.explanation: ## Expressing worry, fear, or distress This function lets you communicate that you feel scared, anxious, or in distress. At A1 level, you only need a few simple phrases. ### Key phrases - Aiuto! — *Help!* (urgent cry for help) - Ho paura. — *I am scared.* - Ho paura di + [noun/infinitive] — *I am afraid of...* e.g. Ho paura dei cani. (*I am afraid of dogs.*) - Sono preoccupato/a. — *I am worried.* (use preoccupato if you are male, preoccupata if female) - Mi fa paura. — *It scares me.* ### Register These phrases work in both formal and informal situations. Aiuto! is always appropriate in an emergency. Sono preoccupato/a is slightly more neutral and can be used in everyday conversation. ### Cultural note Italians may express emotion quite openly and directly. It is natural and normal to say Ho paura! without feeling embarrassed. ### Common mistakes - Forgetting to match the adjective: say preoccupata (not preoccupato) if you are female. - Confusing Ho paura (*I am scared* — literally *I have fear*) with English structure. In Italian you 'have' fear, you do not 'be' afraid with the verb essere.

en.tip: Use Fa male! to say something hurts, Ho male (qui)! to point to where it hurts, and Sto male! to say you feel unwell. These three short phrases will cover most situations where you need to communicate pain.
en.why_this_matters: If you get hurt or feel sick in Italy, you need to communicate this quickly and clearly — at a pharmacy, a doctor's office, or with a friend. These phrases are simple but essential for your safety and wellbeing.
en.explanation: ## Expressing physical pain or discomfort ### When to use this function Use these expressions whenever you want to tell someone that you are in pain or feeling physically unwell — for example, at the doctor, in a pharmacy, or in everyday situations with friends or colleagues. ### Key phrases and patterns | Italian | English | |---|---| | Fa male! | It hurts! | | Fa molto male! | It hurts a lot! | | Ho male qui! | It hurts here! | | Ho male alla testa. | My head hurts. | | Ho male alla pancia. | My stomach hurts. | | Ho male alla gamba. | My leg hurts. | | Sto male! | I feel unwell! / I feel sick! | | Sto molto male. | I feel very unwell. | ### How to point to where it hurts Add qui (here) or a body part after Ho male to be more specific: - Ho male **qui**! — It hurts **here**! (point with your finger) - Ho male **alla testa**. — My **head** hurts. - Ho male **al braccio**. — My **arm** hurts. Note: use al before masculine nouns (al braccio, al piede) and alla before feminine nouns (alla testa, alla pancia, alla gamba). ### Register: formal vs informal These phrases work in both formal and informal situations. At a doctor's office or pharmacy, you can use them exactly as they are — they are already polite enough. ### Cultural context In Italy, it is completely normal to be expressive when describing pain. Pointing to the affected area while saying Ho male qui! is very common and helpful, especially when your Italian is still limited. ### Common learner mistakes - **Translating word for word from English:** Do not say ~~Mia testa fa male~~. The correct pattern is Ho male alla testa or Mi fa male la testa. - **Confusing sto male and fa male:** Sto male means *I feel unwell* (general), while Fa male means *it hurts* (something specific is painful). - **Forgetting the article:** Say Ho male alla gamba, not ~~Ho male a gamba~~.

en.tip: Use mi piace to say you like something, or amo to say you love it. Short exclamations like Bello! or Bravo! are great for quick reactions.
en.why_this_matters: Sharing what you like is one of the most natural ways to connect with people. You will use these phrases constantly — when trying food, meeting someone's pet, or talking about hobbies.
en.explanation: ## Saying you love or like something This function lets you express that you enjoy, love, or appreciate a person, place, thing, or experience. ### Key phrases | Italian | English | |---|---| | Mi piace la pizza. | I like pizza. | | Mi piace molto il caffè. | I really like coffee. | | Amo l'Italia. | I love Italy. | | Amo i gatti. | I love cats. | | Questa pizza è buona. | This pizza is good. | | Che bello! | How lovely! | | Bravo! | Well done! / Great! | ### How mi piace works Mi piace literally means 'it pleases me'. The verb changes depending on what you like: - Mi **piace** il gelato. — I like ice cream. (one thing) - Mi **piacciono** i biscotti. — I like biscuits. (more than one thing) At A1 level, focus on mi piace first. You can learn mi piacciono as you progress. ### Using adjectives A simple adjective after è (is) tells people you like something: - È buono! — It's good! - È bello! — It's beautiful / lovely! - È fantastico! — It's fantastic! You can also use these as standalone exclamations: Bello! Buono! Bravo! ### Formal vs informal These phrases work in both formal and informal situations. Mi piace and amo are neutral. Exclamations like Bello! and Bravo! are more casual and warm. ### Cultural note Italians often express appreciation for food and beauty very enthusiastically. Saying È buonissimo! (It's delicious!) or Che bello! when you genuinely enjoy something will always be well received. ### Common mistakes - **Don't say** ~~Mi piace i gelati~~. When the thing you like is plural, say Mi piacciono i gelati. - **Don't confuse** amo (I love) with mi piace (I like). Amo is stronger and is often used for places, passions, and deep feelings.

en.why_this_matters: You will need to express dislikes every day — when ordering food, choosing activities, or talking about preferences. Knowing how to say you don't like something helps you communicate honestly and avoid things you don't enjoy.
en.explanation: ## Saying You Don't Like Something At A1 level, you have two main patterns to express dislike. ### Pattern 1: Non mi piace + noun This is the most common and natural way to say you don't like something. - Non mi piace il caffè. — 'I don't like coffee.' - Non mi piace questo film. — 'I don't like this film.' When talking about plural things, use Non mi piacciono: - Non mi piacciono le olive. — 'I don't like olives.' ### Pattern 2: [Noun] non è buono/a This pattern describes something as 'not good'. It is slightly less direct about personal taste and more about quality. - Questa carne non è buona. — 'This meat is not good.' - Questo vino non è buono. — 'This wine is not good.' Remember: buono changes to buona for feminine nouns. ### Register Both patterns work in informal and formal situations. They are neutral and polite — not rude or overly strong. ### Cultural note In Italy, food is a big topic of conversation. Saying Non mi piace about food is perfectly normal and acceptable. Italians appreciate honesty about taste preferences. ### Common mistakes - **Forgetting agreement:** Non mi piace vs Non mi piacciono — use the plural form for plural nouns. - **Wrong adjective gender:** Say non è buona for feminine nouns (la pizza non è buona), not non è buono. - **Word order:** Always put non before the verb: Non mi piace, never mi non piace.

en.why_this_matters: You will need this function constantly — when something goes right, when you receive good news, or when you enjoy something. Knowing how to express satisfaction makes your Italian sound natural and helps you connect warmly with other speakers.
en.explanation: ## Expressing Satisfaction in Italian ### When to use this function Use this function when you want to show that you are pleased, happy, or satisfied with a situation, an object, a piece of news, or an outcome. It covers moments like receiving a gift, hearing good news, tasting good food, or finishing a task successfully. ### Key phrases and patterns | Italian | English | |---|---| | Che bello! | How lovely! / How great! | | Perfetto! | Perfect! | | Benissimo! | Very good! / Excellent! | | Ottimo! | Excellent! / Great! | | Sono contento/a. | I am pleased / happy. | | Che bello! Ho trovato le chiavi! | How great! I found the keys! | | Sono contenta di questo regalo. | I am happy about this gift. | ### Register: formal vs informal These exclamations are neutral and work in both formal and informal situations. Che bello! and Perfetto! are very common in everyday speech. Sono contento/a is slightly more personal and can be used in both casual and formal contexts. **Note on gender:** contento changes ending depending on the speaker. Men say sono contento; women say sono contenta. ### Cultural context Italians often express emotions openly and enthusiastically. Short exclamations like Che bello! or Perfetto! are very natural and common — do not be afraid to use them. They make conversation feel lively and engaged. ### Common learner mistakes - **Forgetting gender agreement:** Do not say sono contento if you are a woman — use sono contenta. - **Overusing only one phrase:** Try to vary between Che bello!, Perfetto!, and Benissimo! to sound more natural. - **Confusing satisfaction with happiness:** Sono felice (I am happy) is closer to general joy, while Sono contento/a fits better for satisfaction about a specific thing.

en.explanation: ## Asking if someone likes something ### What this function is for Use this function when you want to find out if someone is satisfied or pleased with something — a meal, a place, an activity, or an experience. ### Key phrase | Italian | English | |---|---| | Ti piace? | Do you like it? | | Ti piace [+ noun]? | Do you like [+ noun]? | | Le piace? | Do you like it? (formal) | ### How it works Piacere works differently from the English verb 'to like'. In Italian, the thing that is liked is the subject of the sentence. So Ti piace la pizza? literally means 'Does pizza please you?' — but it translates naturally as 'Do you like pizza?' - Use Ti piace when talking about **one thing**: Ti piace il gelato? - Use Ti piacciono when talking about **multiple things**: Ti piacciono i film italiani? ### Register: informal vs formal - **Informal** (friends, family, peers): Ti piace? - **Formal** (strangers, older people, professionals): Le piace? At A1 level, focus on Ti piace? first. ### Common learner mistakes - ❌ Tu piaci la pizza? — incorrect word order and pronoun - ✅ Ti piace la pizza? - ❌ Ti piace i film? — wrong verb form with a plural noun - ✅ Ti piacciono i film? ### Cultural note Italians often ask Ti piace? after offering food or showing something they are proud of — their home, their city, their cooking. A warm answer like Sì, mi piace molto! ('Yes, I like it a lot!') is always appreciated.

description: Express that something caught your attention or fascinates you. Use 'Interessante!' or similar short reactions to show curiosity.

en.title: Expressing interest in something
en.tip: Use Interessante! or Che interessante! to show that something has caught your attention. You can also say Davvero? ('Really?') right before or after to sound more natural and engaged.
en.why_this_matters: Showing interest keeps conversations alive and makes your Italian-speaking partner feel heard. Even at A1 level, a simple Interessante! signals that you are engaged and encourages the other person to keep talking.
en.explanation: ## Expressing Interest in Something When something surprises you in a positive way or you want to show curiosity, Italian speakers use short exclamations. At A1 level, a single word can do the job perfectly. ### Key phrases | Italian | English | |---|---| | Interessante! | Interesting! | | Che interessante! | How interesting! | | Davvero? Interessante! | Really? Interesting! | | Molto interessante. | Very interesting. | ### How to use them Interessante! is the simplest and most versatile option. You can use it alone as a reaction, or combine it with Davvero? ('Really?') to sound more conversational. Che interessante! is slightly more expressive — the word che here means 'how' and adds emphasis, similar to saying 'How interesting!' in English. You can also describe something as interesting using è interessante ('it is interesting') or molto interessante ('very interesting'). ### Register These expressions work in both formal and informal situations. Interessante! is neutral and safe in any context — with a teacher, a colleague, or a friend. ### Cultural note Italians appreciate an engaged conversation partner. Showing interest with small reactions like Interessante! or Davvero? is a normal and expected part of Italian conversation, not just a filler. ### Common mistakes - Avoid saying nothing at all — silence can feel cold or dismissive in Italian conversation. - Do not confuse interessante with interessato. Interessante means 'interesting' (describing a thing), while interessato means 'interested' (describing a person): Sono interessato a questo. ('I am interested in this.')
