en.title: Saying thank you in Italian
en.tip: The simplest way to say thank you is Grazie. To sound more grateful, say Grazie mille, which means 'thanks a thousand'. Both work in formal and informal situations.
en.why_this_matters: You will need to thank people constantly — in shops, cafés, classrooms, and at home. Knowing how to say thank you politely is one of the first steps to sounding natural in Italian.
en.explanation: ## Expressing gratitude in Italian ### When to use this function Use this function any time you want to thank someone — when they give you something, help you, or do something kind. ### Key phrases | Italian | English | |---|---| | Grazie | Thank you | | Grazie mille | Thank you very much (lit. 'a thousand thanks') | ### How to use them - Grazie is the everyday, all-purpose word for 'thank you'. You can use it alone or add context: - Grazie per l'aiuto. — *Thank you for the help.* - Grazie, sei gentile. — *Thank you, you're kind.* - Grazie mille is stronger and warmer, like 'thanks so much'. It is still natural in both formal and informal settings. ### Register: formal vs informal Both Grazie and Grazie mille are suitable in all registers — you can say them to a friend, a shopkeeper, or a professor without any change. ### Cultural note Italians use Grazie often and naturally. Saying it with a smile is always appreciated. If someone thanks *you*, the typical reply is Prego (*You're welcome*). ### Common learner mistakes - Do not say ★Grazie molto — this is not standard Italian. Use Grazie mille or Grazie tante instead. - Do not skip the thank-you in service situations — Italians consider it polite and normal to thank staff in shops, bars, and restaurants.

en.title: Responding to a thank-you
en.tip: When someone thanks you in Italian, say Prego — it is the most common and natural reply. You can also say Di niente or Figurati to sound warm and friendly.
en.why_this_matters: You will hear 'thank you' constantly in everyday Italian life — in shops, cafés, classrooms, and with friends. Knowing how to reply naturally makes you sound polite and confident right from the start.
en.explanation: ## Responding to a Thank-You When someone says Grazie to you, you need a quick, natural reply. In Italian, these responses are short and easy to learn. ### Key phrases | Italian | English | |---|---| | Prego | You're welcome | | Di niente | It's nothing / Don't mention it | | Figurati | Don't worry about it (informal) | | Si figuri | Don't worry about it (formal) | | Non c'è problema | No problem | ### Formal vs informal Prego works in **any** situation — formal or informal. It is always safe to use. Figurati is **informal** — use it with friends, classmates, or people you know well. Si figuri is the **formal** version — use it with strangers, older people, or in professional settings like a shop or office. Di niente is neutral and friendly — suitable in most everyday situations. ### Cultural note In Italy, responding to thanks is considered basic politeness. Staying silent when someone thanks you can seem cold or rude. A simple Prego with a smile goes a long way. ### Common mistakes - Do not confuse Prego (you're welcome) with Per favore (please) — they are different phrases used in different situations. - Do not say Figurati in formal contexts — use Si figuri instead.

en.title: Ordering and requesting in service situations
en.tip: In a shop, bar, or restaurant, you can ask for things using a few simple patterns. The easiest is just naming what you want and adding per favore. You can also say io prendo or vorrei before the item.
en.why_this_matters: You will need this function every time you shop, eat out, or visit a café in Italy. These are some of the most common real-life interactions you will have as a beginner.
en.explanation: ## Ordering and requesting in service situations ### When to use this function Use this function whenever you want to order or ask for something from a person working in a shop, bar, restaurant, or similar place. This is one of the most practical functions at A1 level. --- ### Key patterns | Pattern | English meaning | |---|---| | [item], per favore | [item], please | | Io prendo [item] | I'll have [item] | | Vorrei [item], per favore | I would like [item], please | **Examples:** - Un cappuccino, per favore. → A cappuccino, please. - Io prendo la pizza margherita. → I'll have the margherita pizza. - Vorrei un chilo di mele, per favore. → I would like a kilo of apples, please. --- ### Register: formal vs informal Vorrei is the most polite and widely recommended pattern — use it in any service situation. The simple noun + per favore pattern is direct but perfectly acceptable in a bar or café. Io prendo is natural and common in restaurants when reading from a menu. --- ### Cultural context In Italian bars and cafés, it is normal and expected to order quickly and directly. Adding per favore is polite, and grazie at the end of the exchange is always appreciated. In restaurants, io prendo is a very natural way to tell the waiter your choice. --- ### Common learner mistakes - **Forgetting per favore:** Without it, a bare noun can sound abrupt. It is a small word that makes a big difference. - **Using voglio instead of vorrei:** Voglio (I want) is grammatically correct but can sound too blunt in a service context. Vorrei (I would like) is much more natural and polite. - **Over-complicating the request:** At A1 level, simple patterns work perfectly. You do not need long sentences.

en.title: Accepting a request without hesitation
en.tip: When someone asks you to do something, you can simply say Sì to agree. You can make your answer warmer or more polite by adding words like certo, subito, or volentieri.
en.why_this_matters: In everyday Italian life — in shops, restaurants, at work, or with friends — people will ask you to do small things all the time. Knowing how to accept quickly and naturally makes you sound confident and polite from day one.
en.explanation: ## Accepting a Request Without Hesitation This function is about saying **yes** when someone asks you to do something. At A1 level, a single word is enough, but small additions make you sound more natural. ### Key phrases | Italian | English | |---|---| | Sì. | Yes. | | Sì, certo. | Yes, of course. | | Certo! | Of course! / Sure! | | Sì, subito. | Yes, right away. | | Sì, volentieri. | Yes, gladly. / With pleasure. | | Sì, nessun problema. | Yes, no problem. | | Ecco a lei / Ecco a te. | Here you go. (formal / informal) | ### When to use this function Use these phrases any time someone makes a request — a friend asking a favour, a customer asking for something in a shop, or a colleague needing help. This is one of the most common and useful things you can say in Italian. ### Register: formal vs informal - Sì, certo and Sì, subito work in both formal and informal situations. - In a shop or restaurant (formal), Sì, subito! is very natural for staff to say. - With friends (informal), Certo! or Sì, nessun problema sounds friendly and relaxed. - Ecco a lei is formal; use Ecco a te with people you address as tu. ### Cultural note Italians often respond with warmth and enthusiasm. A bare Sì alone is grammatically fine but can sound a little flat. Adding certo or volentieri signals willingness and good manners. ### Common mistakes - **Forgetting short extras:** Learners often stop at Sì even when a warmer response would be more natural. Try to add at least one extra word. - **Using subito in the wrong context:** Subito means 'right away' — only use it when you are actually going to do something immediately. - **Mixing up a lei and a te:** Remember, a lei goes with formal Lei, and a te goes with informal tu.

en.tip: When someone asks you to do something and you need to say no, a simple No works, but adding mi dispiace (I'm sorry) sounds more polite. You can also say non posso (I can't) to give a brief reason.
en.why_this_matters: You will often need to decline requests in everyday situations — at school, work, or with friends. Knowing how to say no clearly but politely helps you communicate naturally without seeming rude.
en.explanation: ## Turning down a request This function covers how to **refuse or decline** when someone asks you to do something. At A1 level, a short, direct response is perfectly natural. ### Key phrases | Italian | English | |---|---| | No. | No. | | No, mi dispiace. | No, I'm sorry. | | Non posso. | I can't. | | No, non posso. | No, I can't. | | Mi dispiace, non ce l'ho. | I'm sorry, I don't have it. | ### Register: formal vs informal In both formal and informal situations, mi dispiace softens the refusal and is always a safe choice. A bare No is acceptable between friends but can sound abrupt in formal or service contexts. ### Cultural note Italians often add a brief explanation after refusing — for example, Non posso, ho da fare (I can't, I'm busy). This is not required at A1, but it makes the refusal feel warmer and more natural. ### Common learner mistakes - **Forgetting mi dispiace**: A plain No without any softener can come across as impolite, especially in shops or with strangers. Try to add mi dispiace when in doubt. - **Confusing non posso and non voglio**: Non posso means *I can't* (inability), while non voglio means *I don't want to*. Use non posso for polite refusals. - **Overcomplicating the response**: At A1, a short phrase is enough. You do not need a long explanation.

en.tip: Use the 'we' form of a verb as a question to invite someone to do something with you. For example, Andiamo al bar? means 'Shall we go to the bar?' You can also use it as an enthusiastic statement: Andiamo! means 'Let's go!'
en.why_this_matters: You will need this function constantly in everyday Italian life — suggesting where to eat, what to do, or where to go with friends or colleagues. It is one of the simplest and most social things you can do with the language.
en.explanation: ## Suggesting an activity together This function lets you invite someone to do something with you — a very common and friendly thing to do in conversation. ### Key pattern: question with 'we' The main pattern is to use the **first person plural** (the 'we' form) of a verb and turn it into a question: - Andiamo al bar? — 'Shall we go to the bar?' - Andiamo a casa? — 'Shall we go home?' - Mangiamo insieme? — 'Shall we eat together?' - Usciamo stasera? — 'Shall we go out tonight?' You can also use it as a direct, enthusiastic suggestion without making it a question: - Andiamo! — 'Let's go!' ### Register: formal vs informal This pattern works in both informal and semi-formal situations. With friends, it sounds natural and warm. In a slightly more formal context, you can still use it — it is not rude. ### Cultural note Italians often make spontaneous suggestions to do things together, especially around food and coffee. Saying Andiamo a prendere un caffè? ('Shall we go for a coffee?') is a very normal and friendly invitation. ### Common mistakes - **Using the infinitive instead of the 'we' form:** Learners sometimes say Andare al bar? — this is not correct in Italian for suggestions. Use Andiamo al bar? instead. - **Forgetting the question intonation:** When written, add a question mark. When speaking, raise your voice at the end to make it a suggestion, not a statement.

en.tip: Use Vuoi...? or Prendi...? followed by the item you are offering. These are simple, friendly ways to offer things like food or drinks. Just add the item after the verb.
en.why_this_matters: You will need this any time you want to be a good host or show kindness — at home, at a café, or with friends. It is one of the most common social exchanges in everyday Italian life.
en.explanation: ## Offering something to someone Use this function when you want to give or offer an object — usually food, a drink, or something similar — to another person. ### Key patterns - Vuoi + [object]? — 'Do you want [object]?' (from volere, 'to want') - Prendi + [object]? — 'Will you have / Take [object]?' (from prendere, 'to take/have') **Examples:** - Vuoi un bicchiere d'acqua? — 'Do you want a glass of water?' - Prendi un caffè? — 'Will you have a coffee?' - Vuoi un po' di pane? — 'Do you want some bread?' - Prendi una fetta di torta? — 'Will you have a slice of cake?' ### Register Both Vuoi...? and Prendi...? are informal and work well with friends, family, or people you know. In a more formal situation — for example, as a waiter or in a professional setting — you might hear Vuole...? (the formal 'lei' form), but at A1 level the patterns above are what you need. ### Cultural note Offering food and drink is an important gesture in Italian culture. Refusing an offer is perfectly fine, but hosts may insist warmly. A simple Sì, grazie or No, grazie is all you need to accept or decline. ### Common mistakes - Do not say Vuoi del un caffè? — choose either un or del, not both. Use un caffè for a countable item and del caffè for an uncountable amount. - Do not forget the question mark intonation — your voice should rise at the end to make it sound like an offer, not a statement.

en.title: Greeting someone in Italian
en.tip: Use Buongiorno, Buonasera, or Buonanotte in formal situations, and Ciao with friends or family. Adding a name or title makes the greeting more personal and polite.
en.why_this_matters: Greetings are the very first thing you say when you meet someone, so getting them right creates a great first impression. Knowing when to be formal or informal will help you feel confident in shops, classrooms, and social situations from day one.
en.explanation: ## Greeting someone in Italian Greetings in Italian depend on two things: **the time of day** and **how well you know the person**. ### Formal greetings Use these with people you don't know well, with older people, or in professional settings: - Buongiorno — 'Good morning / Good day' (used until early afternoon) - Buonasera — 'Good evening' (used from late afternoon onward) - Buonanotte — 'Good night' (used when parting at night or before bed) You can add a title to show extra respect: - Buongiorno, signor Verdi! — 'Good morning, Mr Verdi!' - Buonasera, signora Conti! — 'Good evening, Mrs Conti!' - Buongiorno, prof! — 'Good morning, Professor!' (common with teachers) ### Informal greetings Use Ciao with friends, classmates, family, and children. It works both as 'hello' and 'bye': - Ciao, Luca! — 'Hi, Luca!' - Ciao, come stai? — 'Hi, how are you?' ### Register: formal vs informal Using Ciao with a teacher or a stranger can seem rude or over-familiar. When in doubt, choose the formal option — Italians will appreciate the politeness. ### Cultural note In Italy, greetings often come with a handshake in formal contexts, or a kiss on both cheeks between friends and family. The verbal greeting and the physical gesture go together naturally. ### Common mistakes - ❌ Using Ciao with a professor or a new adult acquaintance — use Buongiorno instead. - ❌ Using Buonanotte as a general evening greeting — it is specifically for saying goodnight when someone is going to sleep. - ❌ Forgetting to add the person's name or title — including it makes your greeting sound much more natural in Italian.

en.title: Responding to a greeting
en.tip: When someone greets you, greet them back with the same word or a matching one. If they ask how you are, say 'Bene, grazie' and return the question with 'E tu?' (informal) or 'E lei?' (formal).
en.why_this_matters: You will hear greetings in almost every Italian conversation, from shops to classrooms to the street. Knowing how to respond correctly — and politely return the question — makes a strong first impression.
en.explanation: ## Responding to a Greeting When someone greets you in Italian, you are expected to greet them back and, if asked how you are, to give a brief answer and return the question. This is a key social ritual at every level of Italian life. ### Greeting back Simply mirror the greeting you receive: - Buongiorno! → Buongiorno! *(Good morning!)* - Buonasera! → Buonasera! *(Good evening!)* - Ciao! → Ciao! *(Hi! / Bye!)* - Salve! → Salve! *(Hello! — neutral, slightly formal)* ### Responding to 'How are you?' Common answers to Come stai? (informal) or Come sta? (formal): | Italian | English | |---|---| | Bene, grazie. | Fine, thank you. | | Molto bene, grazie. | Very well, thank you. | | Non c'è male, grazie. | Not bad, thank you. | | Così così. | So-so. | ### Returning the question Always return the question — it shows politeness and interest: - Informal: E tu? *(And you?)* - Formal: E lei? *(And you? — formal)* So a full informal exchange looks like: Bene, grazie. E tu? ### Formal vs informal register Use Ciao only with friends, family, and people your own age or younger. With strangers, teachers, colleagues, or older people, use Buongiorno, Buonasera, or Salve, and address them as signore, signora, or by their title (e.g. professore, dottore). ### Common learner mistakes - **Forgetting to return the question.** In Italian culture, not asking back can seem cold or rude. Always add E tu? or E lei? - **Using Ciao in formal situations.** This is too casual for a shop assistant, teacher, or boss. Use Buongiorno instead. - **Saying only Bene without grazie.** Adding grazie makes your reply sound natural and polite.

en.title: Introducing someone to others
en.tip: Use Questo è (this is) to introduce a person by name. For formal situations, use their title before the name, like il dottor or la dottoressa.
en.why_this_matters: You will need this any time you bring a friend, colleague, or family member into a conversation. Knowing how to introduce people politely — in both casual and formal settings — is a key social skill in Italian.
en.explanation: ## Introducing Someone Use this function when you want to tell one person who another person is — at a party, in an office, or anywhere people meet for the first time. ### Key Patterns **Informal:** Questo è + name - Questo è Marco. — This is Marco. - Questa è Sofia. — This is Sofia. **Formal (with title):** Il / La + title + name - Il dottor Bianchi. — Dr. Bianchi. - La professoressa Greco. — Professor Greco. ### Masculine vs. Feminine Use questo for a man and questa for a woman. Titles also change: - il dottor / la dottoressa (doctor) - il professor / la professoressa (professor / teacher) - il signor / la signora (Mr. / Mrs.) ### Register - **Informal:** Questo è Luca, il mio amico. (This is Luca, my friend.) - **Formal:** Le presento il dottor Rossi. (Let me introduce Dr. Rossi to you.) — This more formal phrase goes beyond the basic A1 patterns but is useful to recognise. ### Cultural Note In Italy, using titles when introducing people in professional settings shows respect. Dropping a title in a formal context can seem rude. In casual settings, first names alone are perfectly natural. ### Common Mistakes - **Forgetting gender agreement:** Questo è Anna ✗ → Questa è Anna ✓ - **Keeping the article before a title with a name:** In formal introductions, the article (il / la) is used before the title, but it is dropped when directly addressing the person: Dottor Rossi (not Il dottor Rossi) when speaking to them.

en.title: Introducing yourself
en.tip: To introduce yourself in Italian, say Mi chiamo or Sono followed by your name. In formal situations, add a greeting like Buongiorno before your name. Both forms are natural and correct.
en.why_this_matters: Introducing yourself is one of the very first things you do when meeting someone new — at school, at work, or in everyday life. Getting this right from the start helps you make a good first impression in Italian.
en.explanation: ## Introducing Yourself in Italian ### What this function is for Use this function any time you need to tell someone your name for the first time — meeting a new classmate, checking in at a hotel, starting a phone call, or introducing yourself to a teacher. ### Key phrases | Italian | English | |---|---| | Sono Anna. | I am Anna. | | Mi chiamo Marco Rossi. | My name is Marco Rossi. | | Buongiorno, sono la signora Bianchi. | Good morning, I am Mrs Bianchi. | | Buonasera, mi chiamo Luca. | Good evening, my name is Luca. | ### Two patterns that mean the same thing - **Sono** + name — literally 'I am [name]'. Short and natural in both formal and informal situations. - **Mi chiamo** + name — literally 'I call myself [name]'. Also very common and natural. Both are correct. You can choose either one freely. ### Formal vs informal In informal situations (with friends or people your own age), just say Sono Luca or Mi chiamo Luca. In formal situations (meeting a teacher, a doctor, or in a professional setting), add a greeting first: Buongiorno, mi chiamo Marco Rossi. Using your first **and** last name also sounds more formal. ### Cultural note Italians often shake hands when introducing themselves, especially in formal or professional contexts. Making eye contact is considered polite and friendly. ### Common learner mistakes - ❌ Io sono chiamato Marco. — This is a word-for-word translation from English ('I am called Marco') and sounds unnatural. Use Mi chiamo Marco instead. - ❌ Saying only your name without any verb (like just 'Marco') may sound abrupt. Use the full pattern, especially at first. - ✅ Both Sono and Mi chiamo are correct — do not feel you need to pick just one forever.

en.title: Responding when you meet someone
en.tip: When someone introduces themselves or is introduced to you, say Piacere — it means 'nice to meet you'. You can add your own name right after: Piacere, sono [name] or Piacere, mi chiamo [name].
en.why_this_matters: You will need this every time you are introduced to a new person — at school, work, or in social situations. Getting this right makes a great first impression and opens the door to further conversation.
en.explanation: ## Responding to an Introduction When someone introduces themselves or introduces another person to you, the standard Italian response is Piacere, which translates as 'pleased to meet you' or 'nice to meet you'. ### Key Phrases | Italian | English | |---|---| | Piacere | Nice to meet you | | Piacere, sono [nome] | Nice to meet you, I'm [name] | | Piacere, mi chiamo [nome] | Nice to meet you, my name is [name] | ### When to Use It Use these phrases any time someone tells you their name or presents another person to you. It is the natural, expected response — similar to saying 'nice to meet you' in English. ### Formal vs Informal Piacere works in **both formal and informal** situations, which makes it very convenient at A1 level. In a formal context, you might follow it with your full name: Piacere, sono Giulia Ferri. In a casual setting, just your first name is fine: Piacere, sono Giulia. ### Cultural Note In Italy, introductions are often accompanied by a handshake in formal or professional settings, and sometimes a kiss on each cheek among friends. The verbal formula Piacere fits all of these contexts. ### Common Mistakes - **Saying nothing**: Some learners forget to respond at all, which can seem rude. Always reply with at least Piacere. - **Confusing Piacere with Per piacere**: Per piacere means 'please' (as in a request). Piacere alone is the greeting. - **Forgetting to give your name**: It is natural and polite to add your name after Piacere, especially in formal situations.

en.tip: When you raise a glass to celebrate, say Cin cin! or Salute! — both mean something like 'Cheers!' You can add a short wish after, like Buon compleanno! or Al nuovo anno!.
en.why_this_matters: Toasts are part of almost every Italian celebration — birthdays, dinners, weddings, and New Year. Knowing this simple phrase helps you join in and feel part of the moment.
en.explanation: ## Making a Toast in Italian ### What this function is for When Italians raise their glasses together to celebrate or mark a special moment, they make a toast. This is a very short, fixed social ritual — you only need one or two words to do it correctly. ### Key phrases | Italian | English | |---|---| | Cin cin! | Cheers! (casual, playful) | | Salute! | Cheers! / To your health! | Both phrases work in almost any situation. Cin cin! is slightly more informal and playful; Salute! is a little more neutral and can also be used in slightly more formal settings. ### Adding a wish You can follow the toast with a short phrase: - Cin cin! Buon compleanno! — Cheers! Happy birthday! - Salute! Buon anno! — Cheers! Happy New Year! - Cin cin! Auguri a tutti! — Cheers! Best wishes to everyone! ### Cultural context In Italy, it is considered important to make eye contact when clinking glasses. Not doing so is sometimes seen as bad manners or bad luck. At a table with many people, Italians often try to clink glasses with everyone present. ### Common mistakes Learners sometimes try to translate 'Cheers!' word for word — there is no Italian equivalent of that English word used in this context. Stick to Cin cin! or Salute! — these are the natural, expected expressions.

en.title: Congratulating someone
en.tip: Use short, warm phrases like Bravo! or Molto bene! to praise someone. You can add their name or a short comment to make it more personal. These phrases work in almost any situation.
en.why_this_matters: You will often want to react when a friend passes a test, gets good news, or does something well. Knowing how to congratulate someone helps you sound natural and friendly in everyday Italian conversations.
en.explanation: ## Congratulating Someone in Italian Use this function when you want to praise someone or react positively to their achievement or good news. ### Key phrases - Bravo! / Brava! — 'Well done!' (use Bravo for a male, Brava for a female) - Bravi! — 'Well done!' (to a group) - Molto bene! — 'Very good!' - Complimenti! — 'Congratulations!' / 'Well done!' - Ottimo! — 'Excellent!' ### How to use them These phrases can stand alone as a quick reaction: > Hai superato l'esame? Bravo! — 'You passed the exam? Well done!' You can also add a name or a short comment: > Molto bene, Marco! Sei bravo. — 'Very good, Marco! You are good.' ### Register: formal vs informal Bravo/a and Molto bene are used in both informal and formal situations — with friends, family, teachers, or colleagues. Complimenti! is slightly more formal and is common in written messages too. ### Cultural note In Italy, praise is often expressed with energy and warmth. Repeating or emphasising — for example, Bravo, bravo! or Bravissimo! — sounds very natural and enthusiastic, not excessive. ### Common learner mistakes - Forgetting to match the gender: say Brava to a woman, not Bravo. - Using Bravo for a group — use Bravi instead. - Mixing up Complimenti (congratulations / well done) with Auguri (best wishes / happy birthday) — they are not interchangeable.

en.title: Wishing someone well
en.tip: In Italian, most good-wish phrases start with Buon or Buona followed by the occasion or event. Just say the phrase with a smile — no verb needed! The form (Buon vs Buona) depends on the gender of the noun that follows.
en.why_this_matters: Italians exchange good wishes constantly — for holidays, birthdays, trips, and even the start of a new day. Knowing these short phrases will help you sound natural and polite in everyday social interactions right from the start.
en.explanation: ## Wishing Someone Well in Italian This function covers the phrases you use to express good wishes for a special occasion, event, or moment in someone's life. ### Key Phrases Most Italian wish phrases follow a simple pattern: **Buon / Buona + [occasion]** | Italian | English | |---|---| | Buon Natale! | Merry Christmas! | | Buon anno! | Happy New Year! | | Buon compleanno! | Happy birthday! | | Buona Pasqua! | Happy Easter! | | Buone vacanze! | Enjoy your holidays! | | Buon viaggio! | Have a good trip! | | Buona giornata! | Have a good day! | ### Buon or Buona? The word changes to match the gender of the noun: - Use **Buon** before masculine nouns: Buon viaggio, Buon anno, Buon Natale. - Use **Buona** before feminine nouns: Buona Pasqua, Buona giornata. - Use **Buone** before feminine plural nouns: Buone vacanze. ### Responding to a Wish You can reply by repeating the same wish back, or adding anche a te (informal) or anche a lei (formal), meaning 'to you too': - Buon Natale! — Grazie, anche a te! *(Merry Christmas! — Thank you, you too!)* - Buon viaggio! — Grazie mille! *(Have a good trip! — Thank you so much!)* ### Register These phrases work in both **formal and informal** situations. They are short, fixed expressions — you do not need to change them based on who you are speaking to. ### Cultural Note In Italy, wishing people well for occasions is very common and expected. Forgetting to say Buon compleanno to a friend or Buone vacanze to a colleague before the summer break can seem cold. These small phrases show warmth and social awareness. ### Common Mistakes - **Wrong gender:** Saying Buono Natale instead of Buon Natale is a very common error. The form Buon (not Buono) is used directly before a noun. - **Forgetting the plural:** Vacanze is plural and feminine, so it must be Buone vacanze, not Buona vacanze.

en.title: Saying goodbye
en.tip: Use arrivederci in formal or professional situations and ciao with people you know well. You can add a time phrase like a domani to say when you'll meet again.
en.why_this_matters: Every conversation ends with a farewell, so knowing how to say goodbye naturally is essential from day one. Choosing the right word — formal or informal — also shows respect and social awareness.
en.explanation: ## Saying goodbye in Italian Taking leave — or *prendere congedo* — means using the right farewell phrase to close a conversation. The phrase you choose depends on **who you are talking to** and **when you expect to see them again**. ### Formal farewells Use these with strangers, shopkeepers, teachers, or people you address as Lei: - **Arrivederci** — 'Goodbye' (the standard, polite farewell) - **Buongiorno** — 'Good morning / Goodbye' (used when leaving in the morning) - **Buonasera** — 'Good evening / Goodbye' (used when leaving in the evening) - **Buonanotte** — 'Goodnight' (used when parting late at night or before bed) ### Informal farewells Use these with friends, family, classmates — anyone you address as tu: - **Ciao!** — 'Bye!' (very common and friendly) - **Ci vediamo!** — 'See you!' (implies you'll meet again soon) ### Adding a time phrase with a… You can make your farewell more specific by adding a time expression with **a**: | Italian | English | |---|---| | A presto! | See you soon! | | A dopo! | See you later! | | A domani! | See you tomorrow! | | A lunedì! | See you Monday! | These phrases work in both formal and informal contexts. ### Register: formal vs informal Ciao is **informal only**. Using it with a doctor, a professor, or a stranger can seem rude. Stick to arrivederci or a greeting like buonasera in formal situations. ### Cultural note In Italy, farewells are often warm and can include a handshake or a kiss on both cheeks between people who know each other. Even a brief ciao, ciao! (said twice quickly) is very natural and friendly among acquaintances. ### Common mistakes - **Using ciao in formal settings.** Many learners use ciao everywhere because it sounds easy — but in a shop or with an adult you don't know, use arrivederci. - **Forgetting time phrases.** Saying a domani! instead of just ciao sounds more natural and engaged. - **Confusing buongiorno with buonanotte.** Buongiorno is for the morning; buonanotte is only for bedtime or very late at night.

en.tip: When your phone rings, say Pronto to pick up — it means you are ready to talk. You can also say Sì? for a very casual answer. In more formal or professional situations, add your name or the household name after Pronto.
en.why_this_matters: Phone calls are part of everyday life, and the very first word you say sets the tone of the conversation. Knowing how to answer naturally and confidently will help you avoid awkward silences right from the start.
en.explanation: ## Answering the Phone in Italian ### What this function is for This function covers what you say the moment you pick up the phone. In Italian, answering the phone has its own fixed expressions that are different from a face-to-face greeting. ### Key phrases | Italian | English | |---|---| | Pronto? | Hello? / Ready (to speak) | | Sì? | Yes? | | Pronto, sono [nome]. | Hello, this is [name]. | | Pronto, casa Rossi. | Hello, Rossi residence. | | Sì, sono io. | Yes, speaking. (lit. Yes, it's me.) | ### The word Pronto Pronto literally means 'ready'. Historically it signalled to the telephone operator that the caller was ready. Today it is simply the standard Italian way to answer the phone, used in both formal and informal situations. It is almost always the first word a native speaker says when picking up. ### Register: informal vs formal - **Informal** (friends, family): Sì? or just Pronto! - **Semi-formal** (someone calling your home): Pronto? or Pronto, chi parla? ('Hello, who is calling?') - **Formal / professional**: Pronto, sono [nome]. or give the company/family name: Pronto, ditta Bianchi. ### Cultural note In Italy it is very common to answer with just Pronto, even on a mobile phone where the caller's name is displayed. Saying Ciao? alone when answering is less standard and can sound slightly odd — save Ciao for after you know who is calling. ### Common learner mistakes - ❌ Saying Ciao? to answer the phone — this can sound unnatural as an opening word. - ❌ Using Buongiorno or Buonasera alone without Pronto — these greetings work in person but feel abrupt on the phone without Pronto first. - ✅ When in doubt, just say Pronto? — it always works.

en.why_this_matters: Every phone call in Italian starts with identifying yourself — it is expected and polite. Without this, the person on the other end will not know who they are speaking to and may ask, which can be awkward for a beginner.
en.explanation: ## Introducing yourself on the phone When making or receiving a phone call in Italian, you are expected to say who you are right away. This is done with a simple formula. ### Key phrase - Sono [nome] — 'I am [name]' / 'This is [name]' The word sono means 'I am', but in this context it works like English 'This is …' on the phone. ### Common patterns | Italian | English | |---|---| | Pronto, sono Marco. | Hello, this is Marco. | | Buongiorno, sono Anna Bianchi. | Good morning, this is Anna Bianchi. | | Salve, sono il signor Rossi. | Hello, this is Mr Rossi. | ### Register: formal vs informal - **Informal:** First name only is fine with friends or family — Ciao, sono Luca! - **Formal:** Use your full name, or add a title — Sono la dottoressa Martini. Begin with Buongiorno or Buonasera rather than Ciao. ### Cultural note Italians almost always open a call with Pronto (literally 'ready'), which is the standard way to say 'Hello?' on the phone. Follow it immediately with your name so the other person is not left wondering. ### Common mistakes - **Do not say** Io sono … — adding io (I) sounds unnatural here. Just use Sono … - **Do not skip your name** — unlike in some cultures, staying silent or saying only Pronto without identifying yourself can seem rude or confusing in a formal context.

en.tip: To ask if someone is available on the phone, say C'è followed by the person's name. This is the most common and simple way to ask for someone at A1 level. You can add per favore to sound polite.
en.why_this_matters: Phone calls are part of everyday life in Italy — calling a friend, a shop, or an office. Knowing how to ask for the right person is one of the first things you need to do on any call.
en.explanation: ## Asking to speak with someone on the phone When you call someone in Italy, one of the first things you do is ask if the person you want is available. At A1 level, this is very simple. ### Key pattern - C'è [name]? — 'Is [name] there?' This is short for C'è [name] (lì / in questo momento)?, meaning 'Is [name] there (right now)?' ### Examples | Italian | English | |---|---| | Pronto, c'è Marco? | 'Hello, is Marco there?' | | C'è la signora Ferretti? | 'Is Mrs Ferretti there?' | | C'è il dottor Bianchi? | 'Is Dr Bianchi there?' | ### Register: formal vs informal - **Informal (friends and family):** Just use the first name: C'è Giulia? - **Formal (offices, professionals):** Use a title and surname: C'è la signora Rossi? / C'è il dottor Conti? ### Adding politeness You can add per favore at the end to be more polite: C'è Marco, per favore? ### Cultural note In Italy, phone calls typically begin with Pronto (literally 'ready'), which is the standard word for 'hello' on the phone. It is a good habit to say Pronto before anything else. ### Common mistakes - Do not translate 'Can I speak to…?' word for word. Italians do not say *Posso parlare con…? as often at A1 — C'è…? is much more natural and simpler for everyday use. - Remember that c'è is a contraction of ci è and means 'there is'. Do not confuse it with che (that/which).

en.why_this_matters: Phone calls in Italian require specific social rituals, and knowing how to ask who is calling is essential even at the beginner level. You will need this whenever you answer a call and the caller hasn't identified themselves.
en.explanation: ## Asking who is calling on the phone ### When to use this function Use this function when you answer a phone call and the caller has not told you their name. It is also useful when you pick up the phone on behalf of someone else and need to pass on a message. ### Key phrase | Italian | English | |---|---| | Chi è? | Who is it? / Who's calling? | | Chi parla? | Who's speaking? | | Scusi, chi è? | Excuse me, who is it? (formal) | | Chi è, per favore? | Who is it, please? | ### Register: formal vs informal - **Informal** (friends, family): Chi è? or Chi parla? alone is perfectly natural. - **Formal** (work calls, strangers): add Scusi at the start — Scusi, chi è? — or use Chi parla, per favore? ### Cultural note In Italy, it is common to answer the phone with Pronto! (literally 'ready'). If the caller does not introduce themselves straight away, asking Chi è? is completely normal and not considered rude. ### Common learner mistakes - Do not say Chi sei? on a formal call — this uses the informal tu form and may sound impolite with strangers or in professional contexts. Use Chi è? or Chi parla? instead, which are neutral. - Remember that Chi è? is short and direct. Beginners sometimes try to translate 'Who is calling?' word-for-word, but the simple Chi è? is the most natural choice.

en.title: Asking a caller to hold
en.tip: Say Un momento to ask someone to wait on the phone. You can add per favore to sound polite. It works in both formal and informal calls.
en.why_this_matters: Phone calls move fast, and you will often need a second to fetch someone or find information. Knowing how to ask a caller to wait keeps the conversation going smoothly and sounds natural to Italian speakers.
en.explanation: ## Asking a caller to hold When you are on the phone and need a moment — to call someone else, to look something up, or simply to get ready — you ask the caller to wait. ### Key phrase | Italian | English | |---|---| | Un momento | One moment / Just a moment | | Un momento, per favore | One moment, please | ### How to use it Just say Un momento on its own — it is already complete and polite. Adding per favore makes it a little more formal and courteous: - Un momento, per favore. — *One moment, please.* - Un momento, la passo subito. — *One moment, I'll put you through right away.* - Un momento, chiamo Marco. — *One moment, I'll call Marco.* ### Register: formal vs informal In a **formal** call (office, shop, institution), you might say: - Un momento, la passo subito al dottor Bianchi. — *One moment, I'll put you through to Dr Bianchi right away.* In an **informal** call (friend, family), a simple Un momento! or even Aspetta un secondo! (*Wait a second!*) is perfectly natural. ### Cultural note In Italian phone culture, it is common to briefly explain *why* you are asking the caller to wait — for example, Un momento, lo chiamo (*One moment, I'll call him*). This small extra word keeps the conversation warm and friendly. ### Common mistakes - Learners sometimes say nothing and just go silent — always use Un momento so the caller knows you are still there. - Do not confuse Un momento (asking to wait) with Un attimo, which means the same thing and is equally correct. - Avoid translating 'hold on' literally — there is no direct equivalent; Un momento is the natural Italian choice.

en.title: Ending a phone call
en.tip: To end a phone call in Italian, use a farewell word like Arrivederci or Ciao, or an 'A + time' phrase like A presto. Match your choice to the situation — formal or informal. Keep it short and friendly.
en.why_this_matters: Every phone call needs a clear, polite ending. Knowing how to close a conversation confidently — even at A1 level — helps you sound natural and leaves a good impression with Italian speakers.
en.explanation: ## Ending a phone call in Italian When a phone conversation is finished, you need to say goodbye clearly and politely. In Italian, there are several ways to do this depending on who you are talking to. ### Key phrases **Formal goodbyes** (use with people you don't know well, or in professional situations): - Arrivederci — 'Goodbye' (standard, always safe to use) - Buongiorno — 'Good morning / Goodbye' (used when ending a call in the morning) - Buonasera — 'Good evening / Goodbye' (used in the afternoon or evening) - Buonanotte — 'Good night' (used late at night) **Informal goodbyes** (use with friends, family, or people you know well): - Ciao! — 'Bye!' - Ci vediamo! — 'See you!' **'A + time' phrases** (very common, can be formal or informal): - A presto! — 'See you soon!' - A dopo! — 'See you later!' (same day) - A domani! — 'See you tomorrow!' - A lunedì! — 'See you Monday!' (use any day of the week) ### Register: formal vs informal In Italian, choosing the right level of formality matters. On a phone call with a shop, a doctor's office, or someone you don't know, use Arrivederci or a buon... phrase. With a friend or family member, Ciao or Ci vediamo is perfectly natural. ### Cultural note Italians often use both a farewell word and an 'A + time' phrase together at the end of a call, for example: Arrivederci, a presto! or Ciao, a domani! This makes the goodbye sound warm and complete. ### Common learner mistakes - Using Ciao in a formal phone call — this is too casual in professional or unfamiliar contexts. Use Arrivederci instead. - Forgetting to say anything at all — in Italian phone culture, a clear goodbye phrase is expected before hanging up. - Confusing Buongiorno and Buonasera — Buonasera starts around early afternoon (from about 2 p.m. onwards), earlier than in English.

en.title: Opening a letter, postcard, or email
en.tip: Start your message with a greeting that matches how well you know the person. Use Ciao for friends and Caro / Cara for a warmer opening. For formal writing, add a title like Signor or Professoressa.
en.why_this_matters: Even at A1, you may need to write a short postcard, message, or email in Italian. Choosing the right opening immediately shows respect and sets the right tone for everything that follows.
en.explanation: ## Opening a Written Message in Italian ### When to use this function Use these phrases at the very start of any written communication — a postcard, a text message, an email, or a traditional letter. ### Key phrases and patterns | Italian | English | |---|---| | Ciao [Nome] | Hi [Name] | | Caro [Nome] | Dear [Name] (to a male) | | Cara [Nome] | Dear [Name] (to a female) | | Mio caro [Nome] | My dear [Name] (to a male) | | Mia cara [Nome] | My dear [Name] (to a female) | | Caro Signor [Cognome] | Dear Mr [Surname] | | Cara Professoressa [Cognome] | Dear Professor [Surname] | ### Informal vs formal **Informal** (friends, family, classmates): Ciao Luca! or Cara Sofia, — simple and warm. **Formal** (teacher, boss, stranger): Caro Signor Martini, or Cara Dottoressa Conti, — use the title and surname, never the first name. ### Register note Mio caro / Mia cara is affectionate and old-fashioned. You will often see it in letters to close family members or in traditional postcard writing. ### Punctuation In Italian letters and emails, a comma follows the opening greeting: Cara Giulia, — just like in English. ### Common learner mistakes - Using Caro for a woman — remember: Caro = male, Cara = female. - Writing the first name after a formal title: ✗ Caro Signor Marco → ✓ Caro Signor Rossi. - Forgetting the comma after the opening greeting.

en.title: Signing off a message or letter
en.tip: Use a short, warm phrase just before your name to close your message. Choose a friendlier phrase like Baci for family or close friends, and Con affetto when you want to sound a little warmer but still polite.
en.why_this_matters: Even at beginner level, you will want to text, email, or send postcards in Italian. Knowing how to close a message naturally makes your Italian feel complete and genuine.
en.explanation: ## Closing a letter, postcard, message, or email When you finish writing in Italian, you need a short closing phrase before your name — just like 'Love,' or 'See you soon,' in English. ### Key closing phrases - A presto — 'See you soon' — friendly and very common - Ciao — 'Bye' — very informal, fine for friends - Baci — 'Kisses' — warm, for close friends and family - Un bacio — 'A kiss' — slightly softer version of Baci - Con affetto — 'With affection' — warm but a little more polished ### Combining phrases You can easily combine two closings for a fuller goodbye: - Baci e a presto! — 'Kisses and see you soon!' - Un bacio, a presto! — 'A kiss, see you soon!' ### Register: informal vs formal All the patterns here are **informal** — they suit messages to friends, family, and people you know well. For a formal letter or email (to a teacher, a company, etc.), you would use different phrases such as Cordiali saluti ('Kind regards') or Distinti saluti ('Best regards'), but those belong to higher CEFR levels. ### Cultural note Italians are generally warm in written communication even with people they do not know very well. Con affetto can appear in messages to acquaintances, not just close friends. Baci and Un bacio are typically reserved for family and close friends. ### Common mistakes - **Forgetting the closing altogether.** In Italian messages, skipping the sign-off can feel abrupt — always add at least Ciao or A presto. - **Using Baci in formal contexts.** Save it for people you are genuinely close to. - **Writing Con affetto as Con affeto** — remember the double ff.

en.title: Listing and enumerating items
en.tip: To list things in Italian, name each item separated by a comma, then use e ('and') before the last one. This is exactly like making a list in English.
en.why_this_matters: You will need to list things constantly at A1 level — describing a room, ordering food, or saying what you have in your bag. Mastering this simple pattern lets you say a lot with very little grammar.
en.explanation: ## Listing and Enumerating This function lets you **develop a topic by listing its parts or elements** — naming several things one after another to build up a fuller picture. ### The basic pattern In Italian, you list items the same way as in English: > **Item, item, item e item** Separate each item with a comma, and place e ('and') before the **last** item. **Examples:** - In camera c'è un letto, una sedia e un armadio. — 'In the bedroom there is a bed, a chair and a wardrobe.' - Prendo un caffè, un cornetto e un succo. — 'I'll have a coffee, a croissant and a juice.' - Ho uno zaino, un libro e una matita. — 'I have a backpack, a book and a pencil.' ### When to use this Use this pattern any time you want to mention **more than one thing** about a topic: - Describing what is in a place (a room, a bag, a shop) - Ordering food or drinks - Saying what you need or want - Introducing the members of a group (family, friends) ### Register This pattern works in **both formal and informal** situations — listing is the same whether you are chatting with a friend or speaking to a shopkeeper. ### Watch out: e → ed When the next word starts with a vowel, e can become ed to make pronunciation smoother: - un cane ed un gatto — 'a dog and a cat' This is optional at A1 level, but you will hear it often. ### Common learner mistake Do **not** put e between every item the way some languages do. Only one e goes before the **last** item: - ✗ un letto e una sedia e un armadio - ✓ un letto, una sedia e un armadio

en.tip: Use è + adjective to describe what something is like, or c'è to say what is present somewhere. Chain several short sentences together to build up a fuller picture.
en.why_this_matters: Being able to add descriptive detail is essential for talking about your home, town, family, or daily life — all very common topics at A1 level. Without it, your sentences stay too short and listeners cannot picture what you mean.
en.explanation: ## Developing a topic by describing This function lets you **expand on a subject** by adding descriptive information — what something looks like, what qualities it has, or what is found there. ### Key patterns | Pattern | Example | Meaning | |---|---|---| | … è + adjective … | La mia camera è grande. | My room is big. | | C'è + noun phrase … | C'è un parco vicino a casa mia. | There is a park near my house. | | … sono + adjective … | I miei amici sono simpatici. | My friends are nice. | | Ci sono + noun phrase … | Ci sono due finestre. | There are two windows. | ### How it works To describe a person, place, or thing, link the subject to an adjective with è (is) or sono (are). Remember that adjectives in Italian **agree in gender and number** with the noun they describe: - Il libro è piccolo. (masculine singular) - La borsa è piccola. (feminine singular) - I libri sono piccoli. (masculine plural) To say what exists in a place, use c'è (there is) or ci sono (there are). ### Register These patterns work in **both formal and informal** situations. The same structure fits a classroom presentation and a casual chat with a friend. ### Building a description At A1, a description is simply a **sequence of short statements**. You do not need connecting words like *however* or *moreover* — just add one sentence after another: > La mia città si chiama Torino. È grande. C'è un castello e ci sono molti musei. Le piazze sono belle. > *(My city is called Turin. It is big. There is a castle and there are many museums. The squares are beautiful.)* ### Common mistakes - **Forgetting adjective agreement:** saying la casa è grande ✔ but *la casa è grando* ✘ - **Using ha instead of è:** English speakers sometimes say *la stanza ha grande* — this is wrong. Use è for descriptions. - **Confusing c'è and ci sono:** C'è is for one thing; ci sono is for more than one.

en.title: Correcting yourself mid-sentence
en.tip: When you say the wrong word, use no or scusi / scusa to pause and restart. This tells your listener you are changing what you just said. It is natural and expected — even native speakers do this.
en.why_this_matters: At A1 level you will often reach for a word and then realise it is wrong. Knowing how to self-correct smoothly keeps the conversation going instead of grinding to a halt. It also sounds polite and confident rather than confused.
en.explanation: ## Correcting Yourself in Italian ### What this function is for Sometimes you start saying something and then realise you made a mistake — wrong word, wrong item, wrong name. This function gives you a simple way to back up and say the right thing. --- ### Key patterns | Pattern | Meaning | |---|---| | … no … | … no … (neutral self-correction) | | … scusi, … | … sorry, … (formal self-correction) | | … scusa, … | … sorry, … (informal self-correction) | --- ### How to use them **No** is the simplest option. Say what you started to say, pause, say no, then give the correct version: - Vorrei un caffè… no, un tè, grazie. — 'I'd like a coffee… no, a tea, thanks.' - Abito a Roma… no, a Milano. — 'I live in Rome… no, in Milan.' **Scusi / scusa** adds a small apology, which sounds politer — useful in shops, offices, or with strangers: - Vorrei una matita… scusi, una penna. — 'I'd like a pencil… sorry, a pen.' - Il mio nome è Luca… scusa, Marco. — 'My name is Luca… sorry, Marco.' --- ### Formal vs informal - Use scusi with people you address as Lei (strangers, shop assistants, officials). - Use scusa with friends, classmates, or family. - No works in both contexts. --- ### Cultural note Italians self-correct freely in conversation — it is not embarrassing. A quick scusi or no is all you need. You do not have to explain the mistake or apologise at length. --- ### Common learner mistakes - **Stopping completely** instead of continuing — just say no or scusi and keep talking. - **Using scusi with friends** — switch to scusa in informal situations. - **Confusing scusi (self-correction) with scusi (attracting attention)** — the context makes the meaning clear, so do not worry too much about this.

en.title: Asking what something is called
en.tip: When you don't know the Italian word for something, point at it and ask Come si dice? or Come si chiama?. Gestures are your best friend here — point clearly at the object you mean. Both phrases work in almost any situation.
en.why_this_matters: At A1 level, you will constantly encounter things you don't have a word for yet. Knowing how to ask for the word you need lets you keep the conversation going and learn vocabulary in real time.
en.explanation: ## Asking what something is called At A1 level, your vocabulary is still small. This function gives you a lifeline: you can point at any object and ask for its name. ### Key phrases | Italian | English | |---|---| | Come si dice? | How do you say it? | | Come si chiama? | What is it called? | | Come si dice 'apple' in italiano? | How do you say 'apple' in Italian? | | Come si chiama questo? | What is this called? | ### When to use these phrases Use Come si dice? or Come si chiama? whenever you are pointing at an object and want to know its Italian name. Both phrases are nearly identical in meaning and can be used interchangeably. - Come si dice? literally means 'How does one say it?' and is often used when you want to translate a word from your own language. - Come si chiama? literally means 'What is it called?' and is often used when pointing at a physical object. ### Register: formal vs informal Both phrases are neutral and polite. They work in formal and informal situations — with a teacher, a shopkeeper, or a friend. You do not need to change the phrase depending on who you are talking to. ### The role of gestures Pointing or gesturing at the object is an important part of this function. Italian speakers expect and understand this kind of physical communication. A clear gesture removes any confusion about what you are asking about. ### Common learner mistakes - **Forgetting to gesture.** Without a gesture or context, your listener may not know what object you mean. Always point or hold up the object. - **Using Cosa è? instead.** Learners sometimes ask Cosa è? ('What is it?'), which is understandable but less natural than Come si chiama? for asking the name of something. - **Confusing dire and chiamare.** You do not need to worry too much about the difference — both phrases are correct and widely used.

en.why_this_matters: At A1 level your vocabulary is still very small, so you'll often hit a word you simply don't know yet. This question lets you keep the conversation going and pick up new vocabulary on the spot — an essential survival skill from your very first lessons.
en.explanation: ## Asking for Help with a Word or Phrase Sometimes you know what you want to say but not how to say it in Italian. This function gives you a simple rescue phrase you can use any time. ### Key pattern | Italian | English | |---|---| | Come si dice … in italiano? | How do you say … in Italian? | | Come si dice 'apple' in italiano? | How do you say 'apple' in Italian? | The structure is always the same: Come si dice + the word or phrase you need + in italiano? You can also ask about another language: | Italian | English | |---|---| | Come si dice 'mela' in inglese? | How do you say 'mela' in English? | | Come si dice 'buongiorno' in francese? | How do you say 'buongiorno' in French? | ### Register This phrase works in both formal and informal situations. With a teacher, a shopkeeper, or a friend — it always sounds natural and polite. ### Cultural note Italian speakers generally appreciate it when learners make an effort to ask in Italian rather than switching to English. Using this phrase shows you want to stay in Italian, which will earn you goodwill and encouragement. ### Common mistakes - **Don't say** Come si parla …? — this sounds unnatural. Always use Come si dice …? - **Don't forget** in italiano at the end if the language is not already clear from context — it avoids confusion. - The verb si dice is an impersonal form (literally 'one says'). You don't need to change it — it stays the same for every subject.

en.title: Spelling out a word letter by letter
en.tip: When you need someone to understand exactly how a word is written, spell it out loud using Italian letter names, or break it into syllables. You can also say si scrive ('it is written') before spelling the word.
en.why_this_matters: At A1 level, names, addresses, and new vocabulary can be confusing to hear. Knowing how to spell a word aloud helps you make sure the other person writes it down correctly — a very practical skill from day one.
en.explanation: ## Spelling Out a Word in Italian ### When to use this function Use this when you want to make sure your listener understands the exact spelling of a word — for example, giving your name, an email address, or an unfamiliar word. ### Key patterns - **Letter by letter:** say each letter using its Italian name, separating them with short pauses or hyphens. - C (ci) – A – N (enne) – E → 'C-A-N-E' (dog) - **Syllable by syllable:** break the word into its natural syllables. - CA – NE - **Using si scrive:** introduce the spelling with 'it is written'. - Mamma si scrive M (emme) A doppia M (emme) A → 'Mamma is written M-A double M-A' ### Italian alphabet names (key letters) Some Italian letter names are different from English: - **C** = ci - **G** = gi - **H** = acca - **R** = erre - **S** = esse - **Z** = zeta - **Double letter** = doppia + letter name (e.g. doppia emme for 'mm') ### Register This function is neutral — you use the same spelling technique in both formal and informal situations. The context (giving your name to a receptionist vs. helping a friend) does not change the spelling itself. ### Cultural note In Italian, double consonants are very common and change the meaning of words (e.g. pala vs. palla). Italians are used to spelling out words and will often help you by doing the same. ### Common learner mistakes - **Using English letter names:** Remember that C is ci, not 'see', and G is gi, not 'jee'. Using English names can cause confusion. - **Forgetting double letters:** Always signal a double consonant with doppia — for example, doppia elle for 'll' in bello.

en.title: Saying you didn't understand
en.tip: When you don't catch what someone says, use short words like Scusa?, Come?, or Non ho capito to let them know. This is polite and natural — native speakers do it all the time. It opens the door for the other person to repeat or rephrase.
en.why_this_matters: At A1 level, you will often miss words or whole sentences — that is completely normal. Knowing how to signal this quickly and politely means you stay in the conversation instead of nodding along confused. It also shows respect for the speaker by not pretending to understand.
en.explanation: ## Saying you didn't understand When you miss part of what someone says, you need a quick, polite way to let them know. In Italian, a few very short expressions do exactly this. ### Key phrases | Italian | English | |---|---| | Scusa? / Scusi? | Sorry? / Pardon? | | Come? | What? (lit. 'How?') | | Cosa? | What? | | Che? | What? (very informal) | | Non ho capito. | I didn't understand. | ### When to use these Use any of these expressions the moment you realise you missed or didn't understand what was said. You can use them alone or combine them: - Scusa? Non ho capito. — *Sorry? I didn't understand.* - Come? Puoi ripetere? — *What? Can you repeat?* ### Formal vs informal - Scusa? is informal — use it with friends, classmates, or people your own age. - Scusi? is formal — use it with strangers, shop assistants, teachers, or older people. - Che? is very casual and can sound a little abrupt — best kept for close friends. - Come? and Non ho capito work in both formal and informal situations. ### Cultural note Italians speak at a natural pace and it is perfectly normal to ask for clarification. Saying Non ho capito is not rude — it is honest and helpful. Smiling and adding a short follow-up like Puoi ripetere? ('Can you repeat?') makes the exchange feel warm and natural. ### Common mistakes - **Saying nothing**: Many learners stay silent when they don't understand. Use these phrases instead — silence can seem rude or cause real confusion. - **Using Che? in formal situations**: This sounds too blunt in a shop or with someone you don't know well. Choose Scusi? or Come? instead. - **Confusing Scusa and Scusi**: Remember — Scusi is for formal situations, Scusa for informal ones.

en.title: Asking someone to repeat themselves
en.tip: When you miss or don't understand what someone said, use Scusa? (informal) or Scusi? (formal) alone, or add Puoi / Può ripetere, per favore? for a fuller request. Keeping it polite and brief is perfectly natural.
en.why_this_matters: At A1 level, you will often miss words — speakers talk fast, pronunciation is unfamiliar, or there is background noise. Knowing how to politely ask for a repeat is one of the most immediately useful survival skills you can have.
en.explanation: ## Asking someone to repeat themselves ### What this function is for Use this function when you did not hear or did not understand what someone said and you need them to say it again. It is a basic but essential tool for managing real conversations in Italian. --- ### Key phrases | Italian | English | |---|---| | Scusa? | Sorry? / Pardon? (informal) | | Scusi? | Sorry? / Pardon? (formal) | | Puoi ripetere, per favore? | Can you repeat, please? (informal) | | Può ripetere, per favore? | Can you repeat, please? (formal) | | Scusa, non ho capito. Puoi ripetere? | Sorry, I didn't understand. Can you repeat? | | Scusi, non ho sentito bene. Può ripetere? | Sorry, I didn't hear well. Can you repeat? | --- ### Formal vs informal - Use Scusa and Puoi with friends, classmates, children, or anyone you address as tu. - Use Scusi and Può with strangers, older people, shop staff, or anyone you address formally as Lei. - A quick Scusa? or Scusi? on its own — said with a slightly rising tone — is perfectly acceptable and very common in everyday conversation. --- ### Cultural note In Italian conversation, asking for a repetition is completely normal and not considered rude. Italians generally appreciate the effort you are making to understand, and a polite per favore goes a long way. --- ### Common learner mistakes - **Mixing formal and informal:** Don't say Scusa, può ripetere? — if you use the formal Può, also use formal Scusi. - **Forgetting per favore:** A bare Ripeti! (without per favore or puoi) sounds like a command and can come across as rude. - **Overcomplicating it:** At A1 level, a simple Scusa? is often enough. You do not need a long explanation every time.

en.title: Asking how a word is spelled
en.tip: When you hear a word you don't know how to write, ask Come si scrive …? This is a polite and simple way to get clarification. You can point to the word or say questa parola if you can't repeat it.
en.why_this_matters: At A1 level, you will often hear Italian words — names, streets, products — that you need to write down. Knowing how to ask for the spelling quickly saves you from embarrassing mistakes and helps you learn new vocabulary.
en.explanation: ## Asking how a word is spelled Sometimes you hear a word but are not sure how to write it. This function gives you a simple tool to ask for the spelling. ### Key patterns - Come si scrive …? — 'How do you spell …?' / 'How is … written?' - Come si scrive questa parola? — 'How do you spell this word?' The verb si scrive comes from scrivere (to write). The construction si scrive means 'it is written' and is used for all words. ### Examples in context - Scusi, come si scrive il suo cognome? — 'Excuse me, how do you spell your surname?' - Come si scrive 'zaino'? Con la zeta? — 'How do you spell 'zaino'? With a Z?' - Come si scrive questa parola? Non capisco. — 'How do you spell this word? I don't understand.' ### Register This phrase works in both formal and informal situations. In formal contexts, add scusi (excuse me) at the start. In informal contexts with friends, you can just say Come si scrive? directly. ### Cultural note In Italian, spelling things out loud is common in everyday life — giving a name over the phone, filling in a form, or checking a street sign. Italians often use city names to clarify letters, similar to a spelling alphabet (e.g. Milano for M, Roma for R). ### Common mistakes - Don't say Come scrivi? — this means 'How do you write?' in a general sense, not 'How do you spell this word?' - Don't confuse scrivere (to write) with leggere (to read). Use Come si scrive for spelling, not Come si legge (which means 'How is it pronounced / read?').

en.title: Asking someone to speak more slowly
en.tip: When someone speaks too fast, you can ask them to slow down with a short, polite phrase. Use per favore to keep it friendly. Even one word like Piano! works in informal situations.
en.why_this_matters: At A1 level, native speakers will often talk faster than you can follow. Knowing how to ask them to slow down is one of the most useful survival skills you will need in real conversations.
en.explanation: ## Asking someone to speak more slowly When you cannot keep up with what someone is saying, you can ask them to speak more slowly. This is a very common and completely normal thing to do as a beginner. ### Key phrases | Italian | English | |---|---| | Puoi parlare più piano, per favore? | Can you speak more slowly, please? | | Più piano, per favore. | More slowly, please. | | Piano! / Più piano! | Slow down! / More slowly! | | Può parlare più piano, per favore? | Could you speak more slowly, please? | ### Formal vs informal - With friends or people your own age, use puoi parlare più piano? — this uses tu, the informal 'you'. - With strangers, shopkeepers, teachers, or older people, use può parlare più piano? — this uses Lei, the formal 'you'. - In urgent or very informal moments, just saying Piano! or Più piano! on its own is perfectly natural. ### Useful extras You can add a short explanation to be polite: - Sto imparando l'italiano. — I am learning Italian. - Sono straniero / straniera. — I am a foreigner. - Non capisco bene. — I do not understand well. For example: Puoi parlare più piano, per favore? Sto imparando l'italiano. ### Common mistakes - Do not confuse piano (slowly / softly) with lentamente (slowly). Both are correct, but piano is much more common in everyday speech. - Do not forget per favore — without it, the request can sound a little abrupt, especially in formal situations.

en.title: Asking for a definition or paraphrase
en.tip: When you hear a word you don't know, ask what it means using Che cos'è…? or Cosa significa…?. This helps you check your understanding without stopping the conversation for long.
en.why_this_matters: As a beginner, you will often meet unfamiliar Italian words in class, on signs, or in everyday conversation. Knowing how to ask for a quick definition or paraphrase lets you keep learning in real time instead of staying stuck.
en.explanation: ## Asking for a definition or paraphrase Use this function when you hear or read an Italian word or phrase you do not understand and you want the other person to explain it. ### Key phrases | Italian | English | |---|---| | Che cos'è «la sala da pranzo»? | What is «la sala da pranzo»? | | Cosa significa «affollato»? | What does «affollato» mean? | | Che cosa significa? | What does it mean? | | Che cos'è? | What is it? | ### How to use these phrases - **Che cos'è…?** — Use this to ask what a thing or concept *is*. Put the unknown word or phrase after it, often in quotation marks when writing: Che cos'è «il primo piano»? - **Cosa significa…?** (or **Che cosa significa…?**) — Use this to ask what a word *means*: Cosa significa «stanco»? - Both phrases work in everyday conversation. Che cosa significa? is also perfectly correct; Cosa significa? is the shorter, more common spoken form. ### Register: formal vs informal These questions are neutral and polite in any situation — with a teacher, a shop assistant, a friend, or a colleague. No special changes are needed for formal contexts. ### Cultural note Asking for clarification is seen as a sign of engagement in Italian culture, not as a weakness. Native speakers appreciate that you are trying to understand. A short scusi (formal) or scusa (informal) before your question makes it sound even more natural. ### Common learner mistakes - **Confusing Che cos'è and Cosa significa**: Che cos'è asks for an identity or definition ('What *is* it?'), while Cosa significa asks for a translation or meaning ('What does it *mean*?'). In practice they often overlap, so either is fine at A1 level. - **Forgetting to name the word**: Always include the word you are asking about — for example, Cosa significa «tardi»? — rather than just saying Cosa significa? on its own, which can confuse the listener.
